§1.1.text:
§1.1 establishes the right of judicial access and remedy as the foundation on which every other right in Article I depends. A right that cannot be brought before a court and vindicated is not a constitutional guarantee but a statement of aspiration; this provision converts every substantive right into an enforceable one by giving every person standing to seek legal remedy for any violation of their rights under the Constitution, whether that violation arises from an act or an omission, before an independent and impartial court. Naming the forum as independent and impartial ties the remedy to a court structurally separated from the political branches, so that the body enforcing rights is not the same body whose action or inaction is being challenged.

The design choice that does the most work here is the self-executing clause. Rather than leaving legal aid to ordinary appropriations, the text builds in its own fallback: where the Legislature has not funded adequate legal aid, courts appoint counsel at public expense. This closes a specific gap — a legislature could, through simple underfunding, hollow out the right of remedy for anyone unable to afford counsel, without ever formally denying the right. By making the right self-executing, §1.1 does not wait on the Legislature defined in §3.1 (the body comprising the Assembly and Senate, which originates and passes legislation) to act; the courts themselves supply the remedy if the funding stream fails. This is a direct dependency: the provision contemplates the Legislature's ordinary role in funding legal aid, but it does not make the right contingent on that funding arriving, and it does not transfer any of the Legislature's own procedural deadlines or voting thresholds into this mechanism — the only consequence specified here is judicial appointment of counsel, not legislative default or deemed approval of anything.

The closing sentence — procedural costs may not make the right to a remedy illusory — guards against a second, subtler failure mode: even where a court exists and counsel is available, filing fees, bonds, or other procedural costs could price a person out of the very forum §1.1 opens to them. This is a bad-faith safeguard: a government or litigant could nominally honor the right to appear in court while making the cost of appearing prohibitive, defeating the right in substance while preserving it in form. By forbidding procedural costs from rendering the remedy illusory, the text closes that evasion without specifying a particular fee schedule or enforcement mechanism, leaving the standard itself — illusoriness — as the operative limit. Read alongside §1.10's habeas corpus guarantee, which similarly bars courts from declining to hear a particular class of application, §1.1 performs the general function of keeping courts open and remedies real for every constitutional right, while the more specific provisions in Article I handle the particular contours of specific guarantees; §1.1 is the backstop that makes all of them actionable rather than just stated.

§1.2.text:
§1.2 establishes a pre-political baseline: every person holds an inviolable sphere of personal sovereignty over life, body, and choices, and government authority simply does not operate inside that sphere. This is a Democratic Legitimacy Test provision in the clearest sense — it is not a policy preference subject to ordinary political revision but a structural floor beneath all government action. The operative mechanism is the burden-shifting rule in the second half of the provision: where the boundary between individual sphere and government authority is disputed, the presumption runs in favor of individual liberty, and government — not the individual — bears the burden of demonstrating constitutional authority to act. This inverts the default that might otherwise apply in contested cases, so ambiguity about the scope of government power resolves against the government rather than against the person claiming sovereignty.

The practical effect of this structure is to make the sphere self-enforcing in contested cases without requiring a separate enumeration of what falls inside it. Rather than listing protected activities, §1.2 states a governing presumption and places the evidentiary burden on the actor seeking to justify intrusion. This satisfies the Actor Test by naming government as the party that must act — and bear the burden — whenever the boundary is contested, with the consequence of inaction or failure to carry that burden being that the individual-liberty presumption controls. The provision names no specific body to adjudicate this burden, so the mechanism depends on whatever institution hears the dispute.

§1.2's relationship to §1.16 shows how the floor behaves under emergency conditions: §1.16 states that no emergency suspends the Individual Sovereignty Floor in full, meaning the sphere survives even a declared emergency, though rights other than those specifically protected under §1.16.a may be temporarily derogated through the declaration process set out there, with its own 14-day limit, statutory continuation requirement, and bar on renewal. That structure keeps the full suspension of §1.2 off the table while still allowing bounded, published, time-limited derogation of lesser rights — the emergency mechanism cannot be used as a backdoor to erase the floor itself. §1.10's habeas corpus guarantee operates as a related but separate application of sovereignty concerns to detention specifically, with its own 72-hour statutory ceiling and judicial-hearing guarantee; it does not alter or extend §1.2's own burden-shifting rule, since each provision's trigger and consequence stay with the text that states them. Read together, these provisions guard against the failure mode of government expanding its own authority by default — by making contested boundary questions resolve toward liberty and by walling off the sovereignty floor from wholesale suspension even when emergency derogation of other rights is permitted.

§1.3.text:
§1.3 embodies the principle that certain floor rights are pre-political and absolute rather than subject to the ordinary balancing that governs most liberties. The text states the prohibition twice over, first as a categorical bar ("absolutely prohibited") and then in operative terms naming who it binds — agents or officers of the Republic, and any person acting at the Republic's direction or with its acquiescence. There is no exception clause, no proportionality test, and no carve-out for emergency or security justification written into the provision itself. That absoluteness is the design choice: unlike rights that can be weighed against competing interests, this one is built to resist weighing altogether, which is what the Democratic Legitimacy Test asks of truly pre-political restrictions — they cannot be relitigated as policy preference.

The provision's structure was deliberately rebuilt around who is acting rather than where the person is standing. It originally protected only persons "within the Republic's jurisdiction," a territorial test that mirrors language which produced real-world disputes elsewhere over offshore detention, black sites, and extraordinary rendition — a government's own agents operating outside its borders being exactly the scenario a bad-faith reading of "jurisdiction" would exploit against the strongest protection in the document. The current text closes that route by asking who is acting, not where the person is: the bar reaches any agent or officer of the Republic wherever located, and it extends to anyone acting at the Republic's direction or with its acquiescence, which closes the outsourcing option of handing a person to a third party or a foreign government's interrogators while no Republic hand is ever directly involved. An earlier version also carried a redundant "under any circumstances" qualifier, which was later removed as duplicative of the non-derogable framework governing this right — the absoluteness is carried by that framework rather than by extra words in §1.3 itself.

Within Article I, §1.3 sits beside other absolute prohibitions like §1.4's bar on slavery and forced labor, both phrased as unconditional bars rather than rights subject to derogation language. §1.3 is paired with the non-refoulement guarantee, which independently bars returning a person to territory where they face genuine risk of persecution, torture, or deprivation of life — a related protection against torture reached through removal rather than direct infliction, but one that still carried the older territorial phrasing ("within the Republic's jurisdiction") after §1.3 had already moved to an actor-based test, producing an inconsistency between the two that was later identified as running in an unfortunate direction given the non-refoulement provision's role throughout asylum provisions elsewhere in the document. The failure mode §1.3 guards against is precisely the jurisdictional loophole: a state can inflict or outsource torture simply by moving the location of the act, the identity of the hand carrying it out, or the custody arrangement, and a territorial or capacity-limited test would let any of those maneuvers evade the prohibition. By binding the Republic through its agents wherever located and through any proxy acting at its direction or with its acquiescence, the provision denies both the offshoring and the outsourcing escape routes at once.

§1.4.text:
This provision establishes an absolute prohibition on slavery, involuntary servitude, and forced labor, placing it alongside the prohibition on torture as one of the individual sovereignty guarantees in Article I. The word "absolutely" signals that this is a pre-political floor rather than a policy choice subject to ordinary balancing — the state cannot authorize slavery or forced labor as a matter of discretion, and no governmental interest can justify it. This aligns with the constitutional design principle that pre-political restrictions, rather than policy preferences, are what belong in a constitution's rights floor, since control over one's own body and labor is treated as a baseline condition of individual sovereignty rather than something government may adjust by statute or emergency measure.

The design choice embodied in the text is a categorical ban paired with a narrow, enumerated set of exclusions: lawful criminal sentences, jury service, military conscription, and civil emergency duties required by law. By naming these four categories specifically, the provision defines what does not count as forced labor rather than leaving an open-ended public-necessity exception that a bad-faith actor could stretch to cover other compelled labor. The practical effect is that any compulsion to work outside these four named categories is prohibited outright, and the government cannot invent a fifth category by analogy. The clause on private-party labor goes further than the public-duty exceptions: even where government involvement might otherwise be lawful, labor benefiting a private party requires the individual's actual consent. This closes a specific gap — without it, a state could satisfy the forced-labor ban by pointing to a public justification (like a "civil emergency duty") while actually directing the person's labor toward private benefit, such as assigning prisoners or conscripts to work for a private company without their agreement. Requiring consent for private-party labor cuts off that circumvention regardless of what public label is attached to the arrangement.

This provision sits in the same article as the prohibition on torture and cruel treatment, and both share the same absolute, non-balanceable structure — a flat prohibition rather than a standard weighed against government interest. That structural similarity places bodily and labor autonomy in the same category of protection as freedom from torture, both treated as floors beneath ordinary governmental power rather than rights that yield to emergency or necessity. The failure mode the provision guards against is coerced labor dressed up in official or quasi-official justification: criminal sentencing used as a pretext for private exploitation, conscription or emergency duty stretched beyond its named scope, or private employers benefiting from compelled labor while the state looks the other way. By listing the lawful exceptions exhaustively and by isolating private-party labor with its own consent requirement, the text closes off the most likely routes by which forced labor could be reintroduced under another name.

§1.5.text:
§1.5 gathers the core liberties of expression, thought, conscience, religion, association, assembly, petition, and movement into a single provision rather than scattering them across the Article. This reflects the One Home Rule structure: each of these related freedoms lives in one place, so a court or legislature doesn't need to reconcile competing formulations of "expression" or "assembly" scattered across multiple sections. The provision's design embodies the principle that these liberties are pre-political — they are not policy choices subject to ordinary majoritarian adjustment but baseline protections that constrain what government may do regardless of the government of the day's preferences.

The provision's internal structure draws a sharp line between two different risks, and it does so deliberately. Time, place, and manner regulation of expression and assembly is permitted only as necessary for public order and only without viewpoint discrimination — a standard distinct from, and lower than, the scrutiny that would apply to a direct attempt to suppress a message. The reason for this split: the provision originally applied a single, uniformly strict standard to any regulation touching expression or assembly, which meant a parade route restriction or a noise ordinance faced the same exacting test as outright suppression of a viewpoint. That conflated two very different threats. Neutral scheduling and public-order rules are a much smaller category of risk than content or viewpoint discrimination, which is the core danger the right exists to stop, so the current text separates them — a genuine two-tier structure where only the viewpoint-neutral, public-order-necessary category gets the lighter regulatory allowance, while suppression of expression (directly or through intermediaries) and compelled expression are flatly barred without a public-order escape valve. The provision's anti-circumvention language was also tightened: a clause governing when government "has directed" a third party was narrowed to when government "has directed to suppress expression," keeping the prohibition anchored to the specific harm of suppression rather than open-ended direction.

Religion receives its own internal split: belief is protected absolutely, with no exception, while practice is protected unless it causes direct harm to others. This mirrors the belief/conduct distinction common to strong religious-liberty regimes and guards against two opposite failure modes — a government punishing inner conscience (foreclosed entirely) and a government using unregulated "practice" as a shield for harming third parties (checked by the direct-harm exception). The suppress-through-intermediaries clause closes the most obvious bad-faith route around the core prohibition: a government cannot launder censorship through a private platform or proxy and claim it never acted directly. Read against §1.7's independent-judicial-authorization standard for searches and surveillance, and §1.11's trial-rights protections, §1.5 fills the distinct gap those provisions don't cover — the affirmative liberties to speak, believe, assemble, and move — while leaving procedural and privacy protections to their own sections, consistent with keeping each protection in its one proper home.

§1.6.text:
§1.6 establishes the Republic's core equality guarantee: every person stands equal before the law, and government may not discriminate on nine listed grounds — race, ethnicity, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, religion, national origin, disability, and age — plus economic status. This is a pre-political baseline rather than a policy choice subject to ordinary legislative revision: it fixes which categories of government distinction are presumptively suspect, and it does so by tiered scrutiny rather than a flat ban, which lets the provision distinguish between distinctions that threaten equal standing and those that serve legitimate administrative or redistributive purposes.

The structure of the provision does the real work. A distinction based on a listed characteristic triggers compelling justification — strict scrutiny — but two exceptions pull out of that tier: reasonable age standards, and economic distinctions that extend assistance to persons of lesser means. Everything else, meaning distinctions not built on a listed characteristic, need only be rationally related to a legitimate governmental purpose, the ordinary rational-basis floor. The age carve-out exists because age is routinely and legitimately used as a capacity proxy — voting age, licensing minimums, retirement thresholds — and subjecting every such statute to compelling-justification review would make ordinary lifecycle-based governance nearly impossible, while invidious age discrimination still faces the compelling-justification bar. The economic-status carve-out follows the same logic for a different reason: a government obligated elsewhere in the constitution to provide social assistance calibrated to need cannot do so without distinguishing between people who have adequate means and people who don't. Treating every means-tested program as a suspect classification under strict scrutiny would have placed the Republic's own social assistance obligations in tension with its own equality clause, since a program that doesn't ask whether someone already has adequate means isn't assistance at all. The fix splits economic status by direction — distinctions that extend assistance downward get rational basis, other economic distinctions remain subject to compelling justification — rather than exempting economic status from scrutiny altogether, following the same pattern already used for age.

§1.6 connects to the rest of Article I's rights by supplying the anti-discrimination baseline that other provisions invoke rather than restate. §1.16.a's non-derogable rights clause separately voids any emergency measure applied in a discriminatory manner on the basis of race, ethnicity, sex, religion, national origin, sexual orientation, or gender identity — a standalone bar specific to emergency powers rather than a cross-reference to §1.6, since its listed grounds track most but not all of §1.6's list and it omits disability, age, and economic status. §1.5's guarantee of expression, religion, and assembly operates alongside §1.6 without being derived from it. The failure mode §1.6 guards against is government using a facially neutral or categorical rule to entrench disadvantage against a historically vulnerable group while escaping meaningful judicial scrutiny — the tiered structure forecasts that danger by making any listed-characteristic distinction justify itself against a high bar, while still leaving room for age- and need-based governance to function without being treated as the same threat.

§1.7.text:
§1.7 establishes privacy, property, and home security as a single pre-political right held by every person, covering body, home, communications, and data together with the right to own property. The core mechanic is a unified consent-or-warrant rule: government may not enter a home, search a person or property, surveil a person or communication, or collect data unless the person consents or a court issues prior independent judicial authorization grounded in specific, articulable facts. This standard applies territorially within the Republic and extraterritorially to Republic citizens wherever located, so the right travels with citizenship rather than stopping at the border. By naming the judiciary as the checking actor and requiring that authorization precede the intrusion rather than ratify it afterward, the provision satisfies the Actor Test — a holder (every person), a check (prior independent judicial authorization), and an implicit consequence (government action taken without consent or such authorization is outside the government's power). This single consent-or-warrant standard now governs the physical and digital alike, which is why no separate sentence asserting digital-physical equivalence appears: one rule covering "persons, communications, and data" enacts that equivalence structurally rather than declaring it.

The encryption clause and the takings clause are distinct guarantees riding alongside the search rule rather than exceptions to it. "Encryption is lawful and may not be prohibited" forecloses a specific circumvention path: since the surveillance rule already bars warrantless interception of communications and data, a government could otherwise try to reach the same result indirectly by banning the technology that keeps those communications unreadable. Stating the encryption guarantee as an unconditional prohibition — not merely a privacy expectation — closes that route explicitly. The takings clause operates on different subject matter: property may be taken for public use, but only upon just compensation determined independently, pairing the public-use power with a non-negotiable compensation requirement decided by a body other than the government doing the taking. That independence requirement mirrors the architecture of the search rule itself, where an outside judicial actor, not the acting government, supplies the check — the same structural logic of placing a prior independent actor between government and the deprivation it seeks to effect.

This provision previously bundled medical autonomy and bodily non-compulsion together with the privacy and search architecture, and the two families of rights were separated because the bundle concealed a defect: the home ended up protected twice under two inconsistent standards, with one text demanding specific, articulable grounds for searches and another text requiring authorization alone. Splitting the subjects let this provision become single-subject — privacy, property, and home security under one consent-or-warrant rule — while bodily sovereignty was relocated elsewhere. The guarded failure mode is a government that evades meaningful judicial scrutiny by invoking a lesser or inconsistent entry standard, or that defeats the substance of the privacy right by attacking the technology (encryption) that makes privacy practically achievable, or that takes property without a compensation check independent of its own say-so.

§1.8.text:
Section 1.8 establishes the franchise as a personal right rather than a mere procedural arrangement left to ordinary legislation. Every citizen, subject to constitutional eligibility requirements, has the right to vote, stand for office, participate in democratic processes, and have their vote counted. Framing this as an individual right rather than a system of election administration rules means the guarantee sits with the person holding it, not with the officials who run elections, and it ties the franchise to the same rights-bearing structure that protects the other liberties in Article I. The provision then adds a substantive-effects test: no governmental action whose purpose or substantial effect suppresses or reduces access to the franchise is valid. By covering substantial effect and not just purpose, this closes off the common evasion where a facially neutral rule produces the same suppression as an openly discriminatory one — a body cannot achieve indirectly through an administrative burden what it is forbidden to do directly.

The closing sentence sets the provision's operative balance: the Republic must make voting broadly accessible but may not compel voting. These two clauses run in opposite directions and are both binding. The accessibility duty is an affirmative obligation on the Republic, giving it a positive role in removing barriers to voting rather than a passive duty merely to refrain from interference. The companion limit — no compulsion — caps that same duty: the state is required to make the ballot easy to reach, not to force anyone to use it. Read together, these two clauses prevent the accessibility mandate from being used as cover for mandatory voting, while also preventing the non-compulsion clause from being read as license to leave access thin. Each clause checks the other, and the right to have one's vote counted gives the accessibility duty a concrete endpoint: access is not satisfied by mere opportunity to cast a ballot if that ballot is not then counted.

This provision does not police the forum in which citizens assert the right; it defines the right itself, standing apart from the court-access guarantee in §1.1, which addresses remedies for violations of rights generally rather than the franchise specifically. The substantial-effect standard is the provision's main defense against circumvention: it anticipates that suppression often arrives dressed as neutral administration — onerous registration rules, selective closures, or similar mechanisms with a disproportionate exclusionary effect — and it invalidates such action regardless of the label attached to it. The non-compulsion clause guards against the opposite failure mode, where an accessibility mandate is read so expansively that it becomes a justification for state-imposed voting obligations. Together, the three sentences of §1.8 protect the franchise against both direct denial and effect-based erosion while keeping the right to abstain intact.

§1.9.text:
§1.9 establishes an individual right to keep and bear arms for lawful purposes, naming self-defense as its core example, while expressly authorizing the Legislature and the States to regulate how that right is exercised. This is a pre-political guarantee rather than a policy choice left to ordinary majorities — the right itself is fixed in the text, not subject to being voted away, even though its regulatory details are left open to the political process. The structure here is a floor-with-regulation design: the first sentence sets an entitlement every person holds, and the second sentence hands two named regulators — the Legislature and the States — authority over specific regulatory categories: licensing, safety, type, transfer, and carry. That list of regulable subjects is a deliberate boundary on what can be regulated, and the proviso attached to it — "provided lawful ownership for self-defense remains available" — is the floor beneath which regulation cannot sink. Regulators can shape the manner, conditions, and categories of arms-bearing, but they cannot regulate lawful ownership for self-defense out of existence; a regulatory scheme that leaves no path to lawful ownership for self-defense fails the test the provision sets, regardless of what label — licensing, safety, or otherwise — is attached to it.

The provision depends on the Legislature as a defined actor: §3.1 establishes that the Legislature comprises the Assembly and the Senate, with legislation originating in the Assembly and subject to Senate review within a defined window. §1.9 does not borrow any deadline, override, or failure-to-act consequence from that process — it simply names the Legislature as one of two bodies (the other being the States) empowered to regulate arms, leaving the ordinary lawmaking mechanics of §3.1 to govern how that regulatory authority gets exercised into statute. The pairing of national and state regulatory authority in a single sentence means regulation can come from either level without one preempting the other on the face of this text, so long as either source respects the self-defense-ownership floor. This dual-regulator structure, combined with a single named right and a single limiting proviso, keeps the protection in one place rather than scattering self-defense guarantees or regulatory carve-outs across multiple provisions.

The failure mode this provision guards against is a regulatory scheme that uses permissible categories — licensing, safety standards, type restrictions, transfer rules, carry limits — as a backdoor to eliminate the underlying right rather than to shape its exercise. Because the enumerated regulatory powers are broad and could, in bad faith, be stacked to make lawful ownership for self-defense practically unavailable, the proviso functions as the check: regulation is valid only insofar as a path to lawful ownership for self-defense survives it. Without that proviso, the right would be reducible to nothing through sufficiently aggressive licensing or type restrictions; without the regulatory list, the right might be read as near-absolute, foreclosing legitimate safety and transfer rules that the current text clearly permits.

§1.10.text:
Habeas corpus here embodies the pre-political principle that physical liberty cannot be suspended by executive say-so: detention must always be testable before a court that is independent of the detaining authority. The provision names the actor whose liberty is at stake (every person detained by public authority), the check (an independent and impartial court), and the consequence of inaction built into the mechanism itself — a detaining authority that cannot or will not justify the detention within the statutory window loses its claim to hold the person. This is the Actor Test in operation: holder, check, and consequence are all present in the text rather than left to inference.

The specific design choice is a floor-and-delegation structure. The Legislature sets the actual production-and-justification period by statute, but that statute cannot exceed 72 hours — the Constitution fixes the ceiling and leaves the Legislature to set anything tighter. The provision follows a right→floor→delegation pattern, and a stylistic change converted the clause from passive to active voice ("the detaining authority must produce") to match the rest of Article I's drafting style. The practical effect is that no statute, executive order, or administrative practice can stretch the production window past three days, while leaving room for the Legislature to impose stricter deadlines. The third sentence closes off a separate evasion: a court cannot refuse to hear the application at all. Between the ceiling on delay and the bar on judicial refusal, the detaining authority has no procedural gap to exploit — it cannot sit on a detained person indefinitely and it cannot route around review by picking a forum that declines to hear the case.

This provision sits alongside §1.1's general right to legal remedy before an independent and impartial court, but it does its own work: §1.1 guarantees access to court for rights violations generally, while §1.10 guarantees a specific, time-bound mechanism for testing physical detention, with its own non-waivable deadline and its own command that no court may decline the application. That specificity is what distinguishes it from a general remedy clause — a remedy that could be deferred, means-tested, or heard at the court's discretion would not satisfy the function habeas corpus serves. The provision's core failure mode is the use of detention itself as a tool of coercion or concealment, holding someone without ever having to answer for it before a neutral tribunal. By pairing a hard ceiling on the justification window with an absolute duty on courts to hear the application, §1.10 forecloses both halves of that abuse: the authority cannot indefinitely delay accountability, and no court can be used, deliberately or by neglect, as the means of avoiding it.

§1.11.text:
§1.11 embodies the principle that criminal process must be structured to prevent the state's power to prosecute from becoming a tool of coercion rather than a search for truth. The provision bundles together the classic components of fair criminal procedure — prompt notice of charges, publicly funded counsel for those who cannot afford it, adequate time and means to prepare a defense, the ability to examine witnesses, the right to remain silent without that silence counting against the accused, and a speedy trial — because each of these rights depends on the others to be meaningful. Notice without time to prepare is hollow; counsel without the ability to examine witnesses or evidence is powerless; speed without adequate preparation time becomes a trap. The provision also bars increasing a defendant's penalty solely for exercising the right to trial, which closes off a specific pressure tactic: punishing people for refusing to plead guilty by imposing harsher sentences after conviction at trial.

The bail clause does focused, separate work within this same provision. It permits bail only as reasonably necessary to ensure appearance or protect public safety, and explicitly forbids punitive bail. This sets a functional test rather than a fixed amount or category: any bail decision must trace to one of the two permitted purposes, and an amount or condition that serves neither purpose — or that is set simply to punish, deter, or extract hardship before conviction — falls outside what the provision allows. This guards against the specific abuse of using pretrial detention as informal punishment imposed before any finding of guilt, which would hollow out the presumption that an accused person is not yet proven guilty. The closing sentence, granting the accused the right to examine and challenge the evidence against them, including the methods used to produce it, extends the examination right beyond live witnesses to the techniques and processes that generate evidence, guarding against convictions built on unchallengeable forensic or investigative methods.

Several of these guarantees connect to counsel and remedy provisions elsewhere in Article I. The right to counsel at public expense in §1.11 operates alongside §1.1's guarantee that courts appoint counsel at public expense where the Legislature has not funded adequate legal aid, so the obligation to supply counsel is not left dependent solely on legislative appropriation. §1.11 also sits beside §1.12's guarantee of a public trial before an independent and impartial court; §1.11 governs the internal fairness of the proceeding — notice, preparation, confrontation, silence, speed, non-punitive bail, and evidence examination — while §1.12 governs the openness of that proceeding to public scrutiny. Together these two provisions address different failure modes: §1.11 guards against a rigged or coercive process, while §1.12 guards against a secret one. Without §1.11's specific guarantees, an accused person could face charges without adequate warning, be tried without resources to mount a defense, be penalized for insisting on trial rather than pleading, be held in pretrial detention as punishment rather than for appearance or safety, or be convicted on evidence or methods never subject to challenge.

§1.12.text:
Section 1.12 guarantees that a person accused of a crime is tried before an independent and impartial court in a proceeding open to public view. Openness functions as a structural check on the judiciary itself: a trial conducted in public lets anyone observe whether the court is acting independently and impartially, which is the same standard the provision requires of the court. This is a pre-political guarantee about how state power over an individual's liberty is exercised, not a policy choice about criminal procedure — it sits alongside the accused's other trial rights in §1.11 (notice, counsel, speedy trial, confrontation of evidence) but covers a distinct ground: the visibility of the proceeding to the public rather than the procedural entitlements of the accused within it.

The text sets a tight default against secrecy. Closure or sealing of proceedings or records is permitted only to the minimum extent and only for the minimum duration necessary to protect a compelling interest, and that interest must be identified by the court itself — not asserted by a prosecutor or by executive authority. This builds in a graceful degradation path: rather than treating "public trial" as absolute and unworkable in every case, the provision allows narrow, justified departures while keeping the default firmly on disclosure. Every such departure must be published to the NRS, converting what would otherwise be a quiet administrative decision into a public record, and continued secrecy remains subject to independent judicial review, meaning that a closure order is not a one-time grant of permanent concealment but a standing determination that can be revisited. This operationalizes a ceiling on confidentiality — secrecy is never indefinite by default; it persists only as long as the compelling interest persists and continued review bears that out.

The guarded failure mode is a court, prosecutor, or other authority using closed proceedings or sealed records to shield misconduct, bias, or irregular process from scrutiny. Because the compelling interest must be identified by the court and published to the NRS, the justification for closure cannot be asserted and then forgotten; it is logged and remains open to further judicial review rather than resting on an unreviewable initial finding. This provision does not duplicate the specific procedural entitlements of §1.11 — notice, counsel, confrontation, speedy trial — nor the detention-release mechanics of §1.10's habeas corpus right; it occupies its own ground by guarding the transparency of the proceeding itself. The combination of a minimum-necessity standard, a published record of the grounds for closure, and ongoing judicial review means that any narrowing of public access to a criminal trial remains bounded, visible, and subject to correction rather than becoming a permanent or self-certifying exception to the trial's public character.

§1.13.text:
Section 1.13 embodies the pre-political principle of nullum crimen sine lege — no conviction without a pre-existing criminal law and no retroactive worsening of criminal liability for conduct already committed. This is a classic Democratic Legitimacy Test provision: it is not a policy choice subject to ordinary majoritarian adjustment but a structural floor that removes from legislative and judicial reach the power to criminalize past conduct after the fact or to apply a harsher criminal rule backward against an accused person. The text states two distinct guarantees: first, that no person may be convicted for conduct that was not criminal when committed, and second, a broader catch-all that no criminal law may otherwise be applied retroactively to the disadvantage of the accused. That second clause extends beyond the creation of new offenses to cover any retroactive criminal-law change that disadvantages the accused, which could include sentencing or procedural burdens the first clause's conduct-based language alone would not plainly reach.

The actors here are implicit but clear from the Actor Test: the holder of the right is the accused person, the checked actor is any legislature or court applying criminal law, and the consequence of a violation is that the conviction or disadvantageous application cannot stand under this provision's terms. The provision functions independently of the trial-rights provisions nearby — it governs what law may be applied, not how a trial is conducted — so it operates as a distinct layer from §1.11's fair-trial guarantees and §1.12's public-trial guarantee. Its placement alongside §1.14.a, which bars a State or Territory from imposing liability for conduct lawful where it occurred, reflects a shared concern with fixing the legal status of conduct at the time and place it occurred: §1.14.a fixes liability by jurisdiction of occurrence, while §1.13 fixes liability by the law in force at the time of the act. Both provisions prevent a state from reaching backward or sideways to criminalize conduct the actor could not have known was unlawful when it happened, which is the specific failure mode this cluster of Article I protections guards against — governments manufacturing criminal liability after the fact, whether through time (retroactivity) or through jurisdictional relabeling.

The failure mode §1.13 guards against is the core abuse of retroactive lawmaking: a government criminalizing conduct, or increasing its criminal consequences, only after the conduct has already occurred, thereby denying any person fair notice and the chance to conform behavior to known law. Without this provision, a legislature could respond to politically disfavored past conduct by criminalizing it retroactively, or could stiffen penalties and apply them to pending cases, defeating the predictability that criminal law is meant to provide. By fixing the governing law to the moment of the act and barring any application that disadvantages the accused, §1.13 keeps criminal liability anchored to notice given in advance, which is the specific protection that would disappear if this provision were removed.

§1.14.text:
This provision protects a finished criminal judgment from being reopened. Once a person has been finally acquitted or convicted, that outcome is settled, and the state cannot try again or stack additional punishment for the same offense. The provision defines "same offense" with a specific test: the two charges are the same where they arise from the same conduct and the later charge adds no element distinct from the earlier one. This is a conduct-and-elements test, not a bare same-conduct test and not a same-statute test — a second charge survives only if it requires proving something genuinely different from what the first charge required. That precision matters because it fixes the boundary between a barred re-prosecution and a permitted separate prosecution for a genuinely distinct offense arising from overlapping facts.

The provision also addresses the specific case where both a State and the Republic have jurisdiction over the same conduct: both may prosecute, but their sentences do not simply add up. They run concurrently, only the greater term is actually served, and time served under one sentence counts toward the other. This is a deliberate compromise rather than a flat bar on dual prosecution — it lets each sovereign vindicate its own prosecutorial interest in the conduct, but it prevents the practical effect of double jeopardy from reappearing through the back door of cumulative punishment. The person still faces only one real term of confinement, measured by whichever sentence is longer, with credit flowing between the two. This keeps the protection's substance — no double punishment — intact even where the formal bar on double prosecution does not apply.

Within Article I, this provision sits alongside other limits on criminal process: freedom from retroactive criminal law bars punishing conduct that wasn't criminal when committed, while this provision bars punishing already-adjudicated conduct a second time; together they fence in the timing and finality boundaries of criminal liability from two different directions. The companion provision addressing conduct lawful in another jurisdiction operates on a different axis — it limits a State's power to criminalize conduct based on where it occurred, rather than limiting re-prosecution of the same offense — so it does not supply any exception or qualification to this provision's own rules. The failure mode this provision guards against is straightforward: a state using repeated prosecutions, or a second sovereign's parallel prosecution, to multiply punishment or to get a second chance at conviction after losing, by dressing up the same underlying conduct as a new "offense." The elements test closes the trivial version of that evasion — relabeling the same conduct under a different statute — while the concurrent-sentence-with-credit rule closes the version where two sovereigns technically bring separate, non-duplicative charges but the practical punishment still accumulates beyond what either could impose alone.

§1.14.a.text:
§1.14.a bars a State or Territory from punishing a person — civilly or criminally — for conduct that was lawful where it actually took place in another State or Territory, and it extends that same bar to anyone who assisted that conduct or who provided information about it. The rule applies to the forum State's power to impose liability; it does not purport to regulate the State where the conduct occurred, and it does not create any federal offense or remedy of its own. The protection covers three distinct categories in one sentence: the person who engaged in the lawful-where-it-occurred conduct, anyone who assisted that conduct, and anyone who merely provided information about it — all three stand on the same footing against the forum State's liability power.

This provision sits beside the Double Jeopardy and Freedom from Retroactive Criminal Law protections in Article I, and the grouping is functional rather than incidental: all three police a State's or the Republic's power to criminalize or punish conduct after the fact, from different angles. Freedom from Retroactive Criminal Law stops a State from criminalizing conduct that was not criminal anywhere at the time it occurred; §1.14.a stops a State from criminalizing conduct that remains lawful in the place where it occurred, even though the forum State's own law treats it differently. Double Jeopardy, by contrast, polices repeated prosecution for the same offense rather than the conflict-of-laws problem of territorial legality. Read together, these three provisions each guard a separate axis of fair notice and finality in criminal and civil liability, consistent with the One Home Rule principle that each protection should live in exactly one place rather than being re-derived from a neighboring clause.

The specific failure mode this provision guards against is a State reaching across its own borders to punish residents, visitors, or third parties for conduct — or for assisting or merely informing about conduct — that was entirely legal where it happened, effectively exporting its own policy judgments into other States' territory and nullifying the legal effect of acting lawfully elsewhere. Without this rule, a person who traveled to another State or Territory to do something lawful there, or who helped someone do so, or who simply told others about it, could be exposed to liability back home or in a third jurisdiction based solely on the forum's disagreement with the other jurisdiction's law. By fixing liability to the law of the place where the conduct occurred and extending that fixed treatment to assistance and information about the conduct, the provision closes off an indirect route around the underlying lawfulness determination — a route that would otherwise let a State achieve through civil or criminal liability what it cannot achieve by directly regulating conduct outside its own territory.

§1.15.text:
Section 1.15 sits among the individual-rights guarantees of Article I and states a protective floor against material environmental harm, framed the same way several of its neighbors are: it names Government as the restrained actor and sets a limit on what Government may do. The restriction has two parts — Government may not *cause* material environmental harm, and it may not *systematically permit* it either. That second clause closes an obvious evasion: a government could otherwise claim compliance merely by not directly inflicting harm while knowingly tolerating or ignoring a pattern of harm caused by others. By covering systematic permission as well as direct causation, the provision treats sustained inaction or tolerance of harm as a form of the same violation, not a loophole around it.

The provision does not stop at restraining Government passively — it also places an affirmative obligation on the Legislature to establish environmental protections. This routes the duty through the existing lawmaking body defined in §3.1, which comprises the Assembly and Senate and processes legislation through the ordinary bicameral path: bills originate in the Assembly, and the Senate reviews and may amend them within the deadlines set there. Rather than creating a new environmental body or standard-setting authority, §1.15 relies on the Legislature already empowered to make law, leaving the content and specifics of "environmental protections" to statute. The operative constitutional standard is calibrated, not absolute: Government must take "reasonable measures proportionate to known or identifiable harms," and the provision expressly disclaims any guarantee of "a particular environmental outcome." This distinguishes a floor that can actually be met — reasonable, harm-proportionate conduct — from an unworkable mandate that any environmental damage whatsoever constitutes a violation regardless of what was known or foreseeable at the time. The proportionality language ties the obligation to what harms are actually known or identifiable, so the duty scales with available knowledge rather than demanding prediction of every possible harm.

Read alongside §1.6 and §1.5, which occupy the same article and likewise restrain Government from discriminating or suppressing liberties, §1.15 follows the same basic pattern of naming Government as the bound actor and defining the scope of the restriction precisely — here, "material environmental harm to persons or communities," rather than environmental harm in the abstract or harm to ecosystems independent of human effect. The failure mode this provision guards against is twofold: first, a government causing or tolerating serious environmental harm while claiming no violation because it did not act with a single discrete, provable act; and second, a provision so broad that any environmental outcome could be treated as a constitutional breach regardless of reasonableness or available knowledge, which would make the floor impossible to satisfy and invite either paralysis or disregard. The reasonable-and-proportionate standard, paired with the explicit disclaimer against guaranteeing outcomes, keeps the obligation meaningful without converting it into an unbounded mandate over policy results that properly belong to the Legislature's statutory choices.

§1.16.text:
Section 1.16 governs how far emergency power can reach into the rights scheme the rest of Article I establishes, and its central move is to cap the reach rather than trust the emergency's framing. It starts by foreclosing the broadest abuse outright: no emergency suspends the Individual Sovereignty Floor in full, and the six rights listed in §1.16.a — torture, slavery, habeas corpus, public trial, no retroactive punishment, and non-refoulement — are absolute regardless of what the declaration says. Everything else is derogable only through a declaration that states the emergency, the rights affected, the scope, and the duration, published immediately to the NRS. That four-part content requirement, paired with immediate publication, is what makes the derogation checkable at all: a government cannot invoke emergency power quietly or vaguely, because the declaration itself becomes the public record of exactly what was suspended and for how long.

The time structure is built to prevent emergency power from becoming permanent power through inertia. An executive's own declaration runs no more than 14 days — a short, single-actor window suited to genuine immediate need. Anything beyond that requires a statute, moving the decision from one executive to the legislative process, and that statute must carry a fixed expiration; there is no open-ended continuation available at any stage. The provision then forecloses the obvious workaround of letting legislatures or executives extend emergencies indefinitely by serial re-declaration: no declaration or authorization may be renewed or substantially repeated. All emergency measures lapse automatically with their authorization, so nothing survives past the stated deadline by default — the burden is on the state to have acted again through the proper channel, not on the rights-holder to seek restoration.

The provision layers review on top of the time limits rather than relying on them alone. Every declaration gets mandatory expedited independent judicial review, and judicial remedies remain available throughout — language that tracks the same independent-court safeguard found in the Article's habeas corpus and public trial provisions, both of which are themselves non-derogable under §1.16.a. The three Monitors retain full constitutional authority throughout any emergency, meaning the oversight apparatus is not itself something an emergency declaration can touch or suspend. This matters because the Individual Sovereignty Floor, defined in §1.2, places the burden of justifying government intrusion on the government and resolves disputed boundaries in favor of liberty — a presumption that would be hollow if an emergency could simply override it without an independent body checking the declaration's content, scope, and duration. The guarded failure mode is the predictable one: an emergency invoked not for its stated crisis but as a durable tool for suspending rights, extended by repetition rather than renewed by fresh legislative judgment, and insulated from review by executive say-so alone. The provision's publication duty, fixed expirations, non-renewal rule, automatic lapse, and preserved judicial and Monitor authority close off each of those paths in turn.

§1.16.a.text:
§1.16.a embodies the Individual Sovereignty Floor's core commitment: certain rights sit entirely outside the emergency power granted elsewhere in Article I. The parent provision, §1.16, allows either executive to derogate from rights during a declared emergency, but it opens by stating that no emergency suspends the Individual Sovereignty Floor in full, and §1.16.a is what gives that opening sentence content — it names the six rights that remain untouchable no matter what emergency is declared, how it is scoped, or how long it runs. This is a pre-political design choice rather than a policy preference: it does not depend on the merits of any particular emergency, but fixes in advance that torture, slavery, habeas corpus, public trial, the ban on retroactive punishment, and non-refoulement cannot be bargained away by executive or legislative action, however urgent the circumstance.

The design choice here is a hard carve-out rather than a procedural safeguard. Where other Article I rights can be suspended through the §1.16 declaration mechanism — a published statement of emergency, rights affected, scope, and duration, time-limited to 14 days and extendable only by statute with a fixed expiration — the six rights listed in §1.16.a never enter that process at all. The practical effect is that no declaration, however carefully drafted or procedurally compliant, can touch torture, slavery, habeas corpus, public trial, retroactivity, or non-refoulement; any attempt would fall outside what §1.16 even authorizes. The provision also adds a second, independent layer: discriminatory application of any emergency measure on the basis of race, ethnicity, sex, religion, national origin, sexual orientation, or gender identity is void. This is not itself one of the six listed rights but a separate constraint on how any permitted derogation under §1.16 may operate — it governs the manner of emergency measures generally, not just the non-derogable six.

Structurally, §1.16.a depends entirely on its parent for context: it has no independent emergency mechanism of its own, and its force comes from being the named exception inside §1.16's derogation structure. It also depends on the substantive content of the six cited provisions — §1.3's absolute prohibition on torture, §1.4's absolute prohibition on slavery, §1.10's habeas right against detention, and the article-index-named rights to public trial, non-retroactivity, and non-refoulement — each of which defines its own protection once, consistent with keeping each protection in exactly one place rather than restating it here. The failure mode this guards against is the misuse of emergency power to suspend the protections most essential to bodily integrity, liberty, and legal fairness precisely when political pressure to do so is highest; without an absolute, non-negotiable floor, an emergency declaration could otherwise become the vehicle for exactly the abuses — torture, indefinite secret detention, discriminatory targeting, retroactive punishment — that a constitutional rights regime exists to prevent. The void consequence attached to discriminatory application works the same way for a different vector: measures that comply with §1.16's declaration and time-limit requirements on their face could still be used as a tool of targeted persecution against disfavored groups, and declaring such applications void closes that route regardless of how procedurally proper the underlying declaration appears.

§1.17.text:
§1.17 establishes a pre-political entitlement: anyone who reaches the Republic's jurisdiction holds the right to claim asylum and to an independent determination of that claim. The holder is defined by physical presence within jurisdiction, not by citizenship, visa status, or any act of the state recognizing the person — the right attaches automatically upon reaching that jurisdiction. The check is the independent determination required under §6.3, and the consequence of inaction is structural: §6.3(1) specifies that an asylum claim must be determined before removal may be executed, so a state that simply declines to process a claim cannot lawfully remove the claimant in the meantime. This pairing of a bare substantive right in §1.17 with a procedural guarantee in §6.3 keeps the asylum protection in one place for its adjudicative mechanics — adjudicator qualifications, interpreter access, evidence and counsel rights, written decisions, appeal — while §1.17 itself states only the trigger and the entitlement.

The operative design choice in the text is the second sentence: manner of entry does not affect this right. This severs the asylum claim from the lawfulness of how the person arrived, so a person who crosses without authorization holds exactly the same claim and the same right to determination as one who arrives through a formal port of entry. The practical effect reaches into §6.3(3), which forbids imposing any penalty arising solely from irregular entry on a person whose claim is pending or has been granted — the two provisions together mean that irregular entry can be noted but cannot be used as a basis to punish or to short-circuit the claim. §6.3(2) reinforces the same structural point from the other direction: once a federal court grants asylum, residency follows automatically from that determination, without need for State sponsorship or federal certification, so no additional political gatekeeper sits between the court's determination and legal residency.

Read alongside §1.1's general right to legal remedy before an independent and impartial court, §1.17 functions as that same architecture applied to a specific jurisdictional moment — arrival — with §6.3 supplying the specialized procedure (independent courts within the judicial branch, statutory jurisdiction set by the Legislature, appointed counsel where the applicant cannot afford representation) rather than relying on §1.1's general self-executing counsel mechanism. §1.10's habeas framework shows the same pattern of independent-court review with a defined production window for detention, though that 72-hour production rule belongs to habeas detention challenges and is not imported here; §6.3(6) sets its own distinct 72-hour window for appointing a federal legal guardian to an unaccompanied minor, a separate mechanism tied to §1.18 protection rather than to §1.17's entry-point right. The provision's core safeguard is against the bad-faith move of treating an irregular or clandestine arrival as grounds to deny the claim altogether, penalize the claimant, or remove the person before any independent body ever examines the claim.

§1.18.text:
Non-Refoulement establishes an absolute bar on the Republic sending anyone, anywhere, into a territory where genuine risk of persecution, torture, or deprivation of life awaits them. The principle at work is the individual sovereignty floor: certain harms are categorically off-limits regardless of what policy, security, or diplomatic interest might argue for an exception. This is a pre-political restriction in character — it does not weigh the government's reasons against the person's risk; it simply forecloses the action. The provision binds not only the Republic's own agents but "anyone acting at its direction or with its acquiescence," which means the state cannot launder the prohibited act through a proxy, a contractor, or a cooperating foreign government and thereby escape the rule. The scope is also deliberately unqualified by location — "wherever located" — so the protection travels with the person's exposure to the Republic's action rather than stopping at a border or a detention facility's walls.

The provision's most load-bearing sentence is its second one: the protection applies "regardless of the person's status, conduct, or the receiving government." This closes off the most predictable workaround — the argument that a person's immigration status, criminal record, or any other conduct strips them of protection, or that the character of the receiving government (however allied, however trusted) justifies waiving the risk assessment. By naming status, conduct, and receiving government together, the text forecloses three distinct rationalization paths at once: you cannot deny the protection because someone is undocumented or unlawfully present, because they did something wrong, or because the destination government gives assurances. The guard is structural — it removes the discretion to balance the person's perceived deservingness against the risk, which is precisely the balancing a bad-faith actor would try to reintroduce case by case.

This provision sits beside the prohibition on torture and cruel treatment, which binds the Republic and its proxies from inflicting such treatment directly, and the asylum-seeking right named elsewhere in the Article. Non-Refoulement performs a different, complementary function: rather than barring the Republic from inflicting harm, it bars the Republic from delivering a person into someone else's hands to suffer that harm. The "acting at its direction or with its acquiescence" language echoes the torture provision's own phrasing, which keeps the two provisions consistent in how they treat indirect state action — both refuse to let the Republic escape responsibility by outsourcing the harm. Without this provision, the torture prohibition alone would leave a gap: the state could not torture someone itself, but could still hand that person over to a government that would. The failure mode guarded against is exactly that gap — expulsion, extradition, or return used as a mechanism to achieve, through a third party, what direct action is forbidden from achieving, with status or conduct offered as the cover story for doing so.

§2.1.text:
§2.1 establishes the Legat Consul as one half of the dual executive, defining the office by domain, eligibility, and term rather than by a general grant of executive power. The seven-year citizenship requirement is a pre-political qualification tied to the office itself: it sets a threshold of standing in the political community before a person may hold command over military force, foreign affairs, external intelligence, trade agreements, and indigenous nation relations — the specific domain this section enumerates. That enumeration matters structurally because §2.5 defines the Civic Consul's authority as residual: everything not listed here as Legat domain falls to the Civic Consul by default. The two offices are therefore defined as complements of each other, and the phrase "operational decisions within this domain belong to the Legat Consul" marks that, inside the enumerated list, authority is not shared or subject to case-by-case negotiation — it sits with one named actor. The cross-references to §2.3, §2.4, and Article XVI are not independent grants; they point back to this section's domain list, meaning the operational detail of intelligence, trade, and indigenous relations lives in those provisions while the underlying authority and its boundary are fixed here.

The term structure layers three separate limits: a four-year term, a lifetime cap of 12 years in the office, and a rule barring anyone who served any portion of a term — whether by election or by succession — from standing at the next election for that office. Each of these does distinct work. The four-year term sets the ordinary electoral rhythm. The 12-year cap bounds total tenure regardless of how many separate terms or partial terms a person accumulates, and because §2.9(5) counts succession service toward this same 12-year limit, a person cannot extend total time in the office by combining elected terms with periods served as successor. The next-election bar is narrower and separate from both: it applies to the single election immediately following any term in which the person served even partially, closing the specific case where someone exits office — by any means — and immediately seeks to return at the very next contest, rather than barring them from future elections generally. The sentence on immediate transfer of authority upon term expiration guards the gap between terms: there is no interval in which the office's military, foreign-affairs, and intelligence authority sits unheld, which matters given that this domain includes command functions that cannot tolerate a vacancy.

This domain-and-term definition also underwrites §2.9's succession mechanics without itself specifying them: §2.9 governs what happens on death, resignation, or removal, while §2.1 only governs the ordinary case of term expiration and the eligibility and tenure limits that apply whoever holds the office, however they arrived there. The failure mode this section guards against is concentration of unchecked, indefinite executive power over force and foreign relations in one person: the citizenship threshold screens who may hold it, the term and cap bound how long, the next-election bar prevents an immediate return to power after any kind of departure, and the immediate-transfer rule prevents the domain from going ungoverned even for a moment.

§2.2.text:
§2.2 draws a sharp line between inherent defensive authority and authority that requires legislative sanction, and that line is the provision's central structural move. The Legat Consul may act unilaterally only to repel or prevent an active or imminent attack on the Republic's territory, citizens abroad, or treaty allies, including defensive operations crossing the border when that purpose requires it. Anything pursuing other objectives — meaning any military action not justified by that immediate defensive necessity — requires authorization by law within the purposes permitted by §14.1, which confines lawful military force to two categories: protection of territory, citizens, and allies, or, with legislative authorization stating specific grounds, response to crimes against humanity. This mirrors the Institution Test: rather than inventing a new gatekeeping body, the existing Legislature supplies the authorization mechanism for anything beyond immediate defense, and §14.1's requirement that an authorization state which purpose it serves, voiding one that states neither, closes off vague or retroactively-justified military action. The Legat Consul's command authority itself derives from §2.1, which vests military command, force employment, and strategic and tactical determinations in that office as an enumerated domain — §2.2 operates within that grant rather than creating a new one, and the final clause reaffirms that the Legat Consul determines strategy, tactics, and methods within whichever purpose (constitutional defense or statutory authorization) actually applies.

The notification and budget-submission sequence embodies the Transparency Test by forcing every military action into the open through a specific chain: the Legat Consul must notify the Civic Consul and both chamber Speakers upon initiating action, stating purposes and grounds, and must then submit an operational timeline and budget to the Speaker of the Assembly. The provision is explicit that the Civic Consul's notice serves only the exercise of domestic responsibilities and creates no directive authority over military operations — a boundary that tracks §2.5's description of the Civic Consul's domain as residual executive authority over matters not enumerated to the Legat Consul, and that forecloses any reading in which receiving information becomes a foothold for operational control. Operations beyond immediate defensive authority additionally require an authorizing law backed by a plan of action and budget, layering legislative control onto anything that isn't pure repel-or-prevent defense.

The Senate's return-to-alert power is the oversight valve embedded in the framework: by majority vote the Senate can direct that defensive operations stand down once no active or imminent threat justifies continuation, terminating authority for continued active operations — but that termination does not touch the Legat Consul's standing authority to respond immediately to a new or renewed attack, preserving the core defensive power intact. This guards against the failure mode of defensive authority quietly becoming indefinite or mission-creeping war-making without ever passing through the authorization-by-law gate that governs non-defensive objectives, while leaving genuine recurring threats answerable by the same unilateral defensive power each time they arise.

§2.3.text:
§2.3 assigns external intelligence to the Legat Consul as one piece of the broader security portfolio defined in §2.1, which lists military command, force employment, foreign affairs, external intelligence, trade agreements, and indigenous nation relations as the domain where "operational decisions… belong to the Legat Consul." Intelligence direction is accordingly an operational power exercised on the Legat Consul's own authority, not something requiring prior legislative or Senate approval to initiate. That placement reflects the Institution Test: rather than building a separate intelligence oversight body, the constitution routes control through the existing executive office that already holds the rest of the external-security domain, and routes the one necessary check through the existing judiciary rather than a new entity.

The operative design choice is the split between two classes of intelligence targets. Operations against foreign nationals outside Republic territory remain within the Legat Consul's own authority, subject only to a briefing obligation to the Senate, and the text leaves the form of that briefing to be worked out by "the Legat Consul and the Senate" themselves — there is no fixed statutory procedure, deadline, or format specified. Operations against Republic citizens, by contrast, are carved out entirely: the text states flatly that no such operation "may be conducted on the Legat Consul's authority" and that it instead "require[s] independent judicial authorization." This is not a heightened version of the same executive power — it is a removal of that power from the Legat Consul altogether for this category of target, placing the authorizing function with the judiciary instead. The phrase "wherever located" closes the obvious evasion that citizenship-based protection could be sidestepped by acting abroad; the restriction is pegged to the citizen's status, not to geography. This structurally guards against the failure mode of an executive intelligence service turning its tools inward on the citizenry it governs, using the pretext of foreign operations to surveil domestic opponents — a concern the Bad-Faith Test lens makes visible: without the judicial-authorization requirement, the Legat Consul's broad operational discretion over "external intelligence" could otherwise be stretched to cover citizen targets simply by invoking the same authority used against foreign nationals.

§2.3 sits beside §2.3.a, which gives the Legat Consul a security-domain veto over legislation including external intelligence matters — a reminder that the Legat Consul's authority in this domain is substantial elsewhere, which sharpens why the citizen-surveillance carve-out needed to be an outright bar rather than a procedural hurdle the Legat Consul could still absorb or override. It also connects to §2.1's grant of "operational decisions" generally, since §2.3 operates as the specific limit on that general operational grant for one defined category of action. Unlike the briefing arrangement for foreign-national operations, which is left to negotiation between the Legat Consul and the Senate, the citizen protection is not left to inter-branch arrangement at all — it is a fixed structural bar enforced by requiring independent judicial sign-off before such an operation can proceed.

§2.3.a.text:
This provision gives the Legat Consul a narrow, domain-bound veto that checks legislation only where it touches military operations, external intelligence, treaty obligations, or border security — the security domain that §2.1 places under the Legat Consul's authority. The veto fires when the Consul identifies a genuine constitutional concern within that domain, and it must be exercised by returning the bill within 10 business days of final passage with written grounds. That written-grounds requirement produces a public record of the objection, tying the veto's exercise to a stated constitutional rationale rather than a bare policy disagreement, and the domain limitation keeps the Consul's check from expanding into general legislative review — a structural guard against an executive officer substituting personal preference for constitutional concern in areas outside the office's defined competence. The provision also lets either Speaker request an EM domain assessment, giving the Legislature's own leadership a way to test whether the claimed security-domain concern is genuine before the override vote.

The check-and-balance here runs through the Senate: it may override by a two-thirds vote during that same session, and if it does not, the bill simply lapses rather than being sent back for revision or repassage. This is a harder fallback than the Civic Consul's instrument in §2.7, where an unoverridden veto sends the bill back to the Legislature to pass both chambers again; here, absent override, the matter ends for that session. The veto is also strictly single-use per bill: it may be exercised once, and if the same bill is repassed in a subsequent session, it proceeds without Legat Consul veto at all. That repeat-use rule prevents the Consul from indefinitely blocking legislation across sessions by re-invoking the veto each time the Legislature tries again — the failure mode of perpetual executive obstruction on a bill the Legislature is willing to keep passing.

The provision sits as a carve-out from the general Consular Intelligence authority in §2.3, which gives the Legat Consul direction over external intelligence but also constrains that authority (no intelligence operations against citizens without independent judicial authorization, briefing obligations to the Senate on operations against foreign nationals). The legislative veto in §2.3.a extends the Consul's domain competence into a check on legislation touching that same substantive territory, consistent with the office's defined scope under §2.1 rather than creating an open-ended power. The Senate's role as overriding body relies on §3.5's definition of the Senate as the body of two senators per state that elects its own Speaker and sets its own procedures — the same body the Speaker-request mechanism and the two-thirds override both call on, meaning the Senate's existing structure handles this check without any new institution being created for the purpose. The 10-business-day window, the single-use rule, and the lapse default together ensure the veto's effect is bounded in time, in domain, and in repeatability.

§2.4.text:
Section 2.4 places treaty and trade negotiation squarely inside the Legat Consul's foreign affairs domain, which §2.1 defines as covering military command, foreign affairs, external intelligence, trade agreements, and indigenous nation relations. The provision embodies the Dual Executive's division of labor: foreign-facing authority sits with one office rather than being shared or duplicated, consistent with keeping each protection and each grant of authority in a single place. The design choice is that the Legat Consul "negotiates and concludes" these instruments — the operational, external-facing work belongs entirely to that office — but the text immediately subjects this power to §3.6, meaning conclusion is not the same as legal effect. A concluded treaty or trade agreement does not bind the Republic until the ratification mechanics in §3.6 run: two-thirds Senate ratification for treaties, or absolute majority of both chambers for trade agreements, with neither chamber permitted to amend concluded terms. This split — one actor negotiates, a separate body ratifies — keeps the negotiating function efficient and unified while reserving the legitimating, higher-threshold act to the Legislature, so the Legat Consul cannot unilaterally bind the state by concluding an agreement alone.

The consultation clause is the second load-bearing piece of §2.4. On trade and indigenous agreements bearing on domestic interests, the Legat Consul must consult the Civic Consul before or during negotiation, but the Civic Consul's response is explicitly advisory — it does not carry a veto or a consent requirement. This tracks the Civic Consul's defined domain in §2.5: the Civic Consul holds residual executive authority over functions not enumerated to the Legat Consul, together with a separate right under §2.5(5) to be informed on Legat domain matters creating domestic fiscal obligations or bearing on domestic interests, a right that no classification or domain assertion may defeat. Section 2.4's consultation duty and §2.5's information right work together: the Civic Consul cannot be cut out of matters that spill into domestic policy, civil administration, or social-state concerns, even though final negotiating authority remains with the Legat Consul. Making the response advisory rather than binding preserves the single-actor structure of foreign affairs — the Civic Consul is heard, not empowered to co-decide — while still surfacing domestic-interest considerations before an agreement is concluded.

The guarded failure mode is a Legat Consul negotiating and concluding trade or indigenous agreements that carry domestic fiscal or policy consequences without any domestic-side input, then presenting the Legislature and the Civic Consul with a fait accompli.
