Treaties with recognized indigenous nations under Article XVI are carved out of this withdrawal pathway entirely — they may not be unilaterally withdrawn — which prevents the ordinary treaty-exit mechanism from being used to extinguish those specific obligations outside whatever process Article XVI itself establishes for that relationship.

§3.7.text:
§3.7 sets the default voting rule for how a bill becomes law: an absolute majority of the full seated membership of both chambers, not merely a majority of those present and voting. This is the baseline threshold for ordinary legislation under Article III, and it embodies the Procedural Familiarity principle — rather than inventing a bespoke passage rule for every category of legislation, the Constitution establishes one standard mechanism that applies "unless this Constitution provides otherwise." That qualifying clause is doing real work: it signals that other provisions in the Constitution can and do displace this default with their own thresholds, and §3.7 itself tells you how to read those displacements. When a higher threshold is specified elsewhere, it is counted from the full seated membership of whichever chamber or chambers that other provision names — so a two-thirds requirement in another section means two-thirds of all seated members, not two-thirds of a quorum. The provision closes with a definitional rule for the inverse case: wherever the Constitution calls for a "simple majority" of a chamber, that phrase means a majority of members actually voting, with a quorum present — a materially lower bar than the absolute-majority default, since it is counted against attendance rather than full membership.

The practical effect is that §3.7 functions as the interpretive key for every other threshold-setting provision in the document. It does not itself create the two-thirds ratification rule in §3.6 for treaties, or the two-thirds expulsion rule in §3.4 — it supplies the counting method those provisions rely on once they invoke "full seated membership" or "simple majority." This is a clean example of One Home Rule: the counting methodology for legislative thresholds lives in exactly one place, so every other section that sets a vote requirement can simply state a fraction and a chamber without re-explaining what "full seated membership" or "majority voting" means. It also reflects the Institution Test, in that no separate body or procedure is created to resolve threshold ambiguity — the existing chambers and their recorded membership counts do the work.

The failure mode this guards against is a chamber manufacturing an easier path to passage by counting votes against a shrunken or rotating base — for instance, treating a bill as passed because it cleared a majority of whoever happened to be present on a given day, when the Constitution intended a threshold measured against the whole body. By anchoring "absolute majority" and "higher thresholds" to full seated membership, §3.7 forecloses a scenario where low attendance, a snap vote, or strategic absence lowers the real bar for passing legislation or ratifying something that is supposed to require broad institutional buy-in. The simple-majority definition at the end performs the converse function: it prevents a chamber from treating a "simple majority" clause elsewhere as if it demanded support from the full membership, which would make that lower-threshold option meaningless. Together the two rules keep every numeric threshold elsewhere in the Constitution tethered to a single, unambiguous counting convention.

§3.8.text:
§3.8 establishes a transparency-access rule running from the Legislature to the Monitors, and it embodies the Transparency Test and the Informational Power Test together: the body that makes law cannot hide its own lawmaking process from the body charged with watching it, but the watching body's informational reach into unfinished legislation is itself bounded to prevent that oversight from becoming a second legislative check. The provision does two distinct things, and they should not be collapsed into one rule. First, it bars the Legislature from withholding records, deliberations, votes, or draft legislation from the Monitors — a flat, unconditional disclosure duty covering the full range of legislative activity, not just final enacted text. Second, it limits one specific power of the LM — review of pending legislation — to instances triggered only by a member's request. That second clause is a scope limit on the Monitors' own initiative: the LM cannot reach into a bill still moving through the Assembly or Senate on its own motion, only when a member asks it to.

The practical effect is to separate "the Legislature must not conceal" from "the LM must not freelance." The first clause protects against a legislature that tries to shield its internal workings — deliberations, votes, drafts — from scrutiny by treating them as unfinished or informal and therefore exempt from disclosure; by naming records, deliberations, votes, and draft legislation specifically, the provision closes off each of those as a potential hiding place. The second clause guards against the opposite failure mode: an LM that inserts itself into the legislative process uninterrupted, reviewing pending bills at will and functioning as an unelected check on legislation before it is even passed. Tying LM review of pending legislation to a member's request keeps the initiative for inviting oversight into unfinished work with the elected body itself, consistent with the Legislature's standing as defined in §3.1 (comprising the Assembly and Senate, with legislation originating in the Assembly and passing through Senate review) and with the passage mechanics in §3.7, which describe how a bill actually becomes law.

This provision sits beside §3.4's requirement that bill text be published to the NRS before final passage, but the two serve different stages and audiences: §3.4 governs public disclosure of text nearing passage, while §3.8 governs the Monitors' access to the legislative process as it unfolds, including material that may never reach the publication stage at all. If the disclosure duty in §3.8 were absent, the Legislature could withhold deliberations or drafts under cover of procedural privacy, defeating oversight entirely; if the member-request limit on pending-legislation review were absent, the LM could conduct standing, unsolicited surveillance of in-progress lawmaking, turning an oversight function into an unbounded informational power over an elected chamber. The provision's two clauses together hold both failure modes in check at once.

§3.9.text:
§3.9 establishes the constitutional basis for independent agencies — bodies that sit outside the authority of either executive and, by the operational-independence provision that sits alongside it, outside the authority of the Legislature as well in the exercise of their functions. The core structural move is a split between creation and protection: the Legislature holds the power to establish, alter, or abolish any agency it creates by statute, but once this Constitution itself assigns a function to an independent agency, the Legislature may not impair that function's independence. This tracks the broader principle, visible in the delegation provision, that statutory power never fully escapes legislative control — the Legislature can still alter or abolish an agency it created — but it also marks a boundary: a constitutionally assigned function is insulated in a way a purely statutory one is not. The practical effect is a two-tier structure of independence, ordinary (statutory, legislature-alterable) and constitutional (protected from legislative impairment), governed by a single provision rather than scattered protections for each agency.

The provision's second paragraph fills in governance detail by default: unless the Constitution itself specifies otherwise for a particular agency, statute controls organization, appointments, qualifications, terms, and oversight. This default lets the Legislature design each agency's mechanics without a fresh constitutional amendment, while three fixed guarantees constrain what any such statute can do — leadership serves fixed terms, removal requires conduct, incapacity, or incompetence rather than policy disagreement, and qualification requirements cannot be engineered to screen out candidates for their political or policy views or past criticism of government. The removal standard was previously implemented through more elaborate machinery — a pool-based director-selection system and a defined category of disqualifying conduct — both since stripped out. The pool mechanism was replaced by the current formulation precisely because independence itself is the constitutional guarantee while the appointment mechanics are statutory detail; a separately defined "disqualifying offense" was removed because it never did independent work; the removal decision always came down to whether whoever held removal authority found cause made out, and a supermajority convinced of that would reach the same conclusion with or without a technical label.

The for-cause removal standard and the anti-exclusion qualification rule both guard against the same failure mode from different angles: a Legislature or executive could otherwise hollow out independence informally, either by firing agency leadership whenever its decisions are politically inconvenient, or by writing qualification criteria that exclude anyone who has criticized the government or holds disfavored views, filling the agency with compliant appointees without ever touching the fixed-term or removal language. The provision is tied to the Legislature as defined institutionally by the Assembly-Senate structure, since agency-creating and agency-altering statutes must pass through that ordinary legislative process, and it connects to the delegation provision governing how the Legislature may hand defined statutory authority to these same agencies without divesting itself of ultimate statutory control.

§3.9.a.text:
§3.9.a establishes operational independence as a freestanding guarantee: an independent agency, once established either directly by this Constitution or by statute passed through the Legislature, performs its functions free from direction by either executive and free from legislative control over how it exercises those functions, subject only to the Constitution and applicable law. The provision names its actor precisely — "an independent agency" — and states the check affirmatively as a condition that binds both executives and the Legislature simultaneously, rather than listing independence as a privilege the agency must assert. The practical effect is that neither executive can issue operational directives to the agency, and the Legislature's ongoing relationship with the agency is confined to what the Constitution and statute permit, not to case-by-case interference with how the agency carries out its assigned functions. This tracks a Bad-Faith Test reading: without an express operational shield, a Legislature or executive otherwise entitled to create, fund, or oversee an agency could hollow out its independence informally, through directives or pressure, even while leaving the agency's formal statutory status untouched.

The provision depends structurally on its parent section, which supplies the actual mechanics of that independence — the Legislature may establish, alter, or abolish statutory agencies but may not impair the independence of any function this Constitution itself assigns to an independent agency, and agency leadership serves fixed terms removable only for conduct, incapacity, or incompetence, never policy disagreement. Read together, the parent section builds the structural guarantees of fixed terms and removal-for-cause, while §3.9.a states the operating principle those guarantees exist to protect: once in office, agency leadership is free to exercise its functions without executive or legislative interference, subject to law. The Legislature's own provision (§3.1) clarifies which body sits on the other side of this independence — the Assembly-originated, Senate-reviewed body whose ordinary legislative output, including any statute governing an agency's organization or oversight, remains subject to the operational limit in §3.9.a. The delegation provision reinforces the same boundary from another angle: delegated authority exercised by an agency is subject to the delegating statute and to legislative rescission, but the Legislature's retained statutory control over delegation does not translate into a power to direct how the agency exercises its functions day to day.

The failure mode this provision guards against is a legislature or executive nominally respecting an agency's statutory independence while functionally commandeering its operations — through informal direction, conditional pressure, or selective oversight aimed at policy outcomes rather than conduct or incapacity. By stating independence as an operational condition rather than an organizational label, §3.9.a closes the gap between formal agency status and the substance of day-to-day control, while still leaving the agency bound by the Constitution and by applicable law, so that independence from executives and the Legislature does not amount to independence from the law itself.

§3.10.text:
§3.10 establishes the Republic as a government of enumerated powers rather than general jurisdiction: the Legislature may act only within powers this Constitution assigns to it, plus what is reasonably necessary to carry those assigned powers into effect, and everything else defaults to the States and their local governments. This is the structural core of federalism as a pre-political design choice rather than a policy preference — it fixes the boundary of federal authority in the constitutional text itself rather than leaving it to legislative self-definition. The provision then layers three further constraints onto that enumerated-powers baseline. First, even within valid federal competence, the Legislature may not destroy the States' capacity to govern themselves as self-governing communities — a substantive floor protecting state autonomy that operates independently of whether a given law falls within an enumerated power. Second, federal law prevails over conflicting State or local law only "to the extent of the conflict" and only when the federal law was "enacted within federal competence" — supremacy is conditioned on, not a substitute for, the enumeration requirement. Third, minimum standards may be set only where this Constitution assigns the Republic responsibility for the subject or where necessary to secure Article I rights or another express constitutional obligation, closing off a route by which the Legislature might use "minimum standards" language to reach subjects outside its assigned competence. The bar on directing State or local institutions as instruments of federal administration, absent express constitutional authorization, closes a related avenue: commandeering local government machinery to execute federal policy without going through federal institutions of federal accountability.

The second paragraph addresses how constitutional obligations assigned to federal institutions get discharged. Where the Constitution directs that a federal function, standard, procedure, or framework be established, the default mechanism is statute, unless the Constitution specifies otherwise — this gives the Legislature, defined in §3.1 as comprising the Assembly and Senate, the primary instrument for fulfilling constitutional mandates. Where the Constitution assigns a function to a legislative body, independent agency, or other institution, the Legislature must maintain an institution capable of performing it, and no executive or administrative act may substitute for required legislation. This connects directly to §3.9, which lets the Legislature create, alter, or abolish independent agencies but forbids impairing the independence of a function the Constitution assigns to one, and to §3.11, which lets the Legislature delegate authority within federal competence without divesting itself of that authority. Read together, these provisions keep the Legislature as the accountable source of federal lawmaking even when it delegates execution elsewhere: statute prevails over conflicting delegated action, and delegation can be rescinded.

The third paragraph's resourcing duty — that the Legislature must fund institutions sufficiently to perform assigned duties, with material changes in resources accompanied by a published justification — guards against a particular abuse mode: starving an institution of funds as a backdoor way to disable a function the Legislature cannot lawfully abolish or redirect outright, especially one assigned to an independent agency whose operational independence the Legislature may not otherwise impair. Requiring published justification for material resource changes creates a public record addressing the institution's responsibilities and capacity, making defunding-by-stealth harder to execute without visible justification tied to actual institutional need.

§3.11.text:
Section 3.11 lets the Legislature hand off defined slices of its own lawmaking authority to the Consul or to an independent agency created under §3.9, but only within the bounds of federal legislative competence — the Legislature cannot delegate power it does not itself possess. This is the non-delegation structure familiar to separated-powers systems: lawmaking stays constitutionally anchored in the Legislature while day-to-day execution or technical elaboration can be assigned elsewhere. The operative design choice is that a delegation must state its scope and conditions. That requirement forecloses open-ended or blank-check grants; the delegating statute itself has to specify what authority is being transferred and under what limits, which gives the delegate — and anyone reviewing its conduct — a textual boundary to measure against rather than an undefined reservoir of discretion.

The provision's second design choice is that delegation never divests the Legislature of the authority delegated. Two consequences follow directly from the text: statute prevails over any conflicting exercise of delegated authority, and the Legislature may rescind a delegation at any time. Together these mean the delegate exercises the power at the Legislature's sufferance — it is borrowed, not alienated. If the Consul or an agency acts in a way that conflicts with the governing statute, the statute wins; if the Legislature later decides the delegation was unwise, it can take the authority back without needing the delegate's consent or any special procedure stated here. This keeps ultimate accountability for the scope of federal power lodged in the body that is subject to the ordinary legislative process, even while routine or specialized functions are carried out elsewhere.

The provision depends on §3.9 for one of its two delegation targets: an independent agency must already exist as a body "established by statute" under that section before the Legislature can delegate authority to it, and §3.9.a's operational independence means the agency exercises what it's been given without day-to-day direction from the Legislature or either executive — independence in execution, not immunity from the rescission or conflict rules in §3.11 itself. The dependency on §3.10 (federal legislative competence) is likewise structural: because the Legislature can only legislate within assigned federal powers, any delegation under §3.11 is capped at that same boundary — it cannot manufacture authority beyond what the Legislature already holds. Finally, each exercise of delegated authority must be published to the NRS identifying the delegating statute, so every actual use of delegated power is traceable to the specific statute that authorized it. This guards against the failure mode of an open-ended or silent handoff of lawmaking power — a delegate acting without a defined mandate, or continuing to act after the Legislature's own statute has changed or been rescinded, with no public record tying the exercise back to its source.

§4.1.text:
§4.1 lays out the judiciary's basic architecture: district courts, appellate courts, and the Supreme Court. Only the Supreme Court is named directly by the text; district and appellate courts exist as categories, and the Legislature holds the power to establish, abolish, and define the jurisdiction of inferior courts by statute. This is the Institution Test at work — rather than fixing a permanent lower-court structure in constitutional text, the provision lets the Legislature build and resize the inferior judiciary through ordinary statute, using an existing body (the Legislature, defined in §3.1 as comprising the Assembly and Senate) instead of creating a separate constitutional mechanism for court design. The Supreme Court itself, by contrast, is constitutionally fixed in its existence and structured in detail elsewhere — its minimum size, staggered terms, and quorum rules live in §4.3, not here, consistent with each protection living in exactly one place.

The abolition clause is the provision's most pointed safeguard: when the Legislature abolishes a court, that abolition takes effect, for each occupied seat, only upon expiration of the sitting judge's term. This clause is read against a bad-faith scenario — a Legislature hostile to a particular judge's rulings could not simply abolish that judge's court and remove them mid-term. The judge finishes the term regardless of the statute's effective date for vacant or newly-created seats. This dovetails with §4.2's rule that inferior court judges serve a single non-renewable 12-year term and may be removed only through the misconduct or incapacity processes in §4.2(3) — abolition-by-statute is not an alternate removal track. Without the term-expiration limit, the Legislature's statutory power over inferior courts could function as a backdoor around the removal protections §4.2 establishes, defeating judicial independence through structural rather than direct means.

The final sentence — that constitutional questions arising in any proceeding may be referred to the Supreme Court — connects the inferior court structure to the Supreme Court's role as the body equipped to resolve constitutional questions. This reflects a functional specialization: district and appellate courts handle ordinary proceedings, but when a constitutional question arises within any of them, it can move to the SC, which under §4.3 requires at least five participating justices to resolve constitutional questions specifically (as opposed to the lower ordinary quorum threshold for other matters). The referral mechanic in §4.1 and the participation floor in §4.3 operate at different levels — one is about routing a question, the other about how many justices must sit on it — and nothing in this provision supplies a deadline, procedure, or mandatory-versus-discretionary rule for how or when such referral occurs. Taken together, §4.1 establishes the three-tier architecture, assigns lower-court design to the Legislature by statute, protects sitting judges from mid-term displacement through abolition, and opens a channel for constitutional questions to reach the Supreme Court, while leaving the detailed mechanics of appointment, removal, and Supreme Court composition to the provisions that specifically govern them.

§4.2.text:
This provision embodies judicial independence as a pre-political structural guarantee: once seated, an inferior court judge's tenure, compensation, and decisional freedom are insulated from the ordinary political actors who placed the judge on the bench. The design choice is visible in each clause. Appointment runs through a fixed pipeline — the Civic Consul nominates from the Judicial Pool established under §9.8, and the Senate confirms by a majority of its full seated membership — rather than open nomination, which ties every inferior judge's credentials to the pool's objective eligibility criteria rather than to the nominating or confirming officials' preferences. The term is a single, non-renewable twelve years, which means a sitting judge never has to think about reappointment or currying favor with the Consul or Senate to stay on the bench; paragraph (2) forecloses removal for anything but the paragraph (3) process, and expressly states that disagreement with a decision is not grounds for removal, closing off the most obvious informal pressure point. Paragraph (3) then supplies the only two removal channels: a 2/3 vote of both chambers for serious misconduct, abuse of office, or permanent incapacity, with the Legislature's finding of grounds declared final, or a statutory judicial-discipline process under SC oversight for conduct- or competence-based grounds — and neither requires a prior Monitor finding. Paragraph (4) bars any public official from directing, threatening, or attempting to influence a judge's decision in a pending matter outside the proceeding itself, and locks in compensation against reduction during the term, removing the two cheapest levers — intimidation and the purse — that political actors could otherwise use to bend a ruling.

The provision depends on other parts of the judicial architecture to function. The Judicial Pool it draws from is defined in §9.4.a, which sets eligibility at 15 years of legal practice or 10 years of judicial service, bars a former Supreme Court justice from re-entering the pool, and allows a judge to move to nomination for a different federal court even after serving on one — a career-ladder design that lets district and appellate experience feed upward rather than trapping ambitious candidates out of advancement. The pool mechanics themselves — minimum size, objective-only eligibility, and exclusion-review rights — sit in §9.8, which this provision cites directly rather than restating, keeping pool administration in one place. The Legislature executing removal is the body defined in §3.1, comprising the Assembly and Senate, and the 2/3 concurrent-vote removal standard mirrors the same threshold used for a Supreme Court justice in §4.3.a, giving inferior and high-court removal a matching supermajority bar even though the two offices are addressed separately.

The failure mode this provision guards against is capture of the bench by the political branches, whether through rigged appointments, removal for unpopular rulings, salary retaliation, or direct pressure on a pending case. By fixing a single long term, naming disagreement with a decision as an invalid removal ground, protecting compensation, and prohibiting extra-proceeding influence, the provision prevents the Consul, Senate, or any other official from treating a judge's continued tenure or livelihood as leverage over the outcome of a case.

§4.3.text:
§4.3 establishes the Supreme Court's basic architecture — size, tenure, and the rules for deciding when the Court has spoken at all — and each piece is built to resist manipulation by whoever controls appointments or legislative majorities at a given moment. The statute sets the seat count, but a floor of never fewer than five is fixed in the constitutional text itself, so no ordinary statute can shrink the Court below that number. Raising or lowering the number of seats requires 2/3 of both chambers, a supermajority threshold that keeps court-packing or court-shrinking off the table for a transient simple-majority coalition. The reduction rule goes further: even with a 2/3 vote, a cut in seats takes effect only through attrition, meaning sitting justices cannot be removed from office simply by legislating their seats out of existence. That protects individual tenure from indirect removal and channels any removal of a justice through the only route built for it — the separate misconduct-and-incapacity process in §4.3.a, where the Legislature's finding that grounds exist is final and mere disagreement with a ruling is explicitly not grounds. Single non-renewable 12-year terms in staggered classes, as nearly equal as practicable, mean no single appointing cycle can reshape the whole Court at once and no justice has a renewal incentive that could bend rulings toward the body that controls reappointment.

The second paragraph handles what happens when the Court cannot produce a clear answer or lacks enough participating justices to answer at all. An equally divided Court leaves the challenged ruling in effect, or, in an original proceeding, grants no relief — a default that avoids manufacturing new law or new relief out of a non-result, and the equal division carries no binding precedent, so the tie does not quietly harden into a rule for future cases. Ordinary quorum is a majority of seated justices, and that count explicitly includes a Temporary Associate Justice — the Appellate Court judge who, under §4.4(4), steps in immediately upon a vacancy with full voting rights until the vacancy is filled — so a vacancy alone cannot stall the Court's ordinary business. Constitutional questions, however, require at least five participating justices regardless of how small the ordinary quorum might otherwise run, treating the gravest category of case as needing a wider base of judicial judgment before the Court can act on it at all.

This structure depends on surrounding provisions to function: §4.1 is what actually routes constitutional questions to the Court for decision, §4.4 supplies the confirmation process and the Temporary Associate Justice mechanism that keeps the Court staffed between vacancies, and §4.3.a supplies the only lawful path to remove a sitting justice, closing off any temptation to use the seat-count or term provisions as a backdoor removal tool. The five-justice floor for constitutional questions is treated as the real constitutional minimum for that category of case — a point confirmed when a separately created emergency panel with a lower quorum for military-authority disputes was found to conflict with it and was reworked so the five-justice floor stands unqualified rather than carrying an unstated exception.

§4.3.a.text:
§4.3.a establishes legislative removal of Supreme Court justices as the sole mechanism for ending a justice's tenure outside the natural expiration of the single 12-year term set in §4.3. The design choice is a 2/3 vote of both chambers triggered by serious misconduct, abuse of office, or permanent incapacity, with the Legislature's determination that grounds exist made final. That finality matters structurally: it forecloses any further review of whether the threshold was actually met, so once two-thirds of the Assembly and two-thirds of the Senate agree grounds exist, the removal stands. The provision also states two express limits on how that power can be used — disagreement with a decision is not grounds for removal, and no Monitor finding is a prerequisite to removal — both of which narrow the occasions on which the power may be invoked or shape what triggers it, without disturbing the finality of the Legislature's own determination once it acts on a proper ground.

This structure depends on surrounding provisions without duplicating them. The Legislature itself is defined in §3.1 as the Assembly and Senate acting together, which is why §4.3.a requires action by both chambers rather than a single body — a bicameral threshold consistent with how the Legislature otherwise exercises its gravest powers. The Supreme Court's own definition in §4.3 supplies the office being protected: a justice holds a single non-renewable 12-year term, staggered by class, and removal under §4.3.a is the only route by which that term can end early. The same mechanism — 2/3 of both chambers, grounds limited to serious misconduct, abuse of office, or permanent incapacity, Legislature's determination final, no Monitor finding required, disagreement not grounds — appears essentially verbatim for inferior court judges in §4.2(3), which also offers a second track of statutory judicial-discipline removal under SC oversight that §4.3.a does not include for Supreme Court justices. That parallel shows the same removal design applied symmetrically across the judiciary, with the extra statutory track reserved for inferior judges rather than transferred to the Supreme Court.

The guard embedded in this provision is against two distinct abuse paths. First, "disagreement with a decision is not grounds for removal" blocks the Legislature from using removal as a tool to punish a justice for an unpopular ruling, which would collapse judicial independence into legislative preference. Second, "no Monitor finding is prerequisite to removal" prevents removal from being bottlenecked by, or dependent on, a separate oversight body's prior action — the Legislature can act on its own assessment of misconduct or incapacity without waiting on an external finding. A later change removed a district-court seniority cascade that had been part of this provision's temporary-replacement mechanics, leaving the constitutional authorization for removal itself intact while assigning the administrative detail of filling the resulting vacancy to statute.

§4.4.text:
§4.4 structures Supreme Court appointment as a two-actor process with a built-in bench-continuity mechanism, and it draws every nominee from the Judicial Pool established under §9.8 rather than letting the Civic Consul pick freely. The Civic Consul, whose office holds residual executive authority under §2.5, nominates from among pool members meeting statutory SC qualifications, and must do so within a statutory period capped at 90 days after a vacancy arises. The Senate then votes within a statutory period capped at 120 days after nomination, and confirmation requires a majority of the full seated Senate — not merely those present and voting. The text is explicit that no deemed confirmation applies: Senate silence or delay does not produce a justice by default. This pairs a political nominator with a political confirmer in the same two-actor pattern used elsewhere for senior offices, while denying either actor the ability to force an outcome simply by doing nothing.

The structural problem this leaves open — what happens to the Court's business while nomination or confirmation is pending or stalled — is answered by subsection (4), not by the Senate vote itself. Upon a vacancy, the most senior eligible Appellate Court judge by continuous service becomes Temporary Associate Justice immediately, by constitutional operation, with full voting rights, until the vacancy is filled; ties go to the older judge. This automatic, seniority-based rule removes any discretion over who holds the seat in the interim and ensures the Court never sits short-handed waiting on the political branches. Because the Appellate Court is itself drawn from the same Judicial Pool framework under §9.8, and pool eligibility is fixed by objective, non-ideological criteria under §9.8(3), the temporary justice arrives through the same depoliticized candidate base as a confirmed one, rather than through ad hoc executive selection. Subsection (5) then fixes the term consequence: a justice's term runs from confirmation, and anyone who fills a mid-term vacancy — whether through the ordinary route or, as the sibling public-confirmation mechanism contemplates, through the alternate route triggered by nominating or voting delay — serves only the remainder of the original term rather than a fresh full term. This keeps vacancy-filling from becoming a backdoor way to extend a justice's tenure beyond what the departed justice would have served.

The 90-day and 120-day caps, read together with the no-deemed-confirmation rule, guard against two distinct failure modes: a Civic Consul who simply declines to nominate, and a Senate that refuses to bring a nomination to a vote or deadlocks without rejecting it outright. Because deemed confirmation is barred, the Senate cannot be forced into producing a justice by inaction, but neither can it indefinitely freeze the Court, since the automatic Temporary Associate Justice already occupies the seat with full voting power and the missed-deadline consequence shifts the matter elsewhere. The eligibility baseline itself — drawn from the Judicial Pool's statutory qualifications and the objective-criteria requirement — keeps the nomination pool insulated from exclusion on legal philosophy, temperament, or political association, so the Civic Consul's choice is constrained to a pre-vetted set rather than an open field.

§4.4.a.text:
§4.4.a is a fallback mechanism that activates only when the ordinary appointment process in §4.4 breaks down. Under §4.4, the Civic Consul nominates a Supreme Court justice from the Judicial Pool within a statutory period (capped at 90 days), and the Senate must vote within a statutory period (capped at 120 days), with confirmation by majority of the full seated Senate and no deemed confirmation. If either actor misses its window, the Temporary Associate Justice already sitting under §4.4(4) — the most senior eligible Appellate Court judge who assumed the seat immediately by constitutional operation — is instead submitted to the citizens for public confirmation at the next federal electoral period. This converts a branch-to-branch failure into a direct popular check, giving the people a concrete consequence to act on when the Civic Consul and Senate cannot or will not complete the normal process, rather than leaving the seat in indefinite limbo filled only by an interim judge.

The provision borrows its voting mechanics wholesale from elsewhere rather than inventing new ones. Confirmation requires 60% of votes cast "under §7.3," which is the Constitution's general rule that any supermajority required in a direct citizen vote is 60% of votes cast (outside amendment referendums), so §4.4.a simply plugs into that existing threshold rather than setting its own. Likewise, the statute implementing public confirmation votes must apply §8.1's foreign-contribution prohibition and disclosure regime — full disclosure of contributors and amounts, a bar on anonymous and foreign-sourced contributions, and treatment of coordinated expenditures as direct contributions — to this vote specifically. That cross-application keeps judicial confirmation votes financially transparent and insulated from foreign money using the same architecture already built for electoral campaigns, rather than creating a parallel finance regime unique to this one scenario. The Temporary Associate Justice's express right to advocate publicly for confirmation sits inside that same financial framework, so public campaigning for the seat is permitted but still subject to §8.1's disclosure and foreign-source limits.

The provision also fixes the race condition between the ordinary and public routes: an ordinary nomination and Senate confirmation completed before Elections Panel certification of the ballot ends the public route, so the branches retain a late chance to resolve the vacancy themselves before the election supersedes them, but once certification occurs the public process controls. The outcome rules close the loop — a confirmed justice serves out the remainder of the original term, consistent with §4.4(5)'s rule that a justice filling a mid-term vacancy only completes that term, while a rejected nominee triggers a restart: the next eligible Appellate Court judge becomes Temporary Associate Justice and the vacancy process begins again under §4.4. This guards against a Civic Consul or Senate that stalls the ordinary process indefinitely — whether through inaction, obstruction, or deadlock — by ensuring the seat cannot remain filled only by an unelected interim judge without ever facing either confirming body, Senate or citizenry.

§4.5.text:
Section 4.5 sets the outer boundary of judicial power: what courts may do, what they may not do, and who may bring a case. Subsection (1) gives courts the power to declare legislative acts, executive orders, and administrative decisions unconstitutional and void — the core judicial review function. Subsection (2) immediately fences that power in by confining courts to constitutional and legal questions rather than policy questions, and by directing that ambiguous statutes be read consistently with the Constitution without permitting courts to rewrite clear statutory text. This keeps judicial review interpretive rather than legislative. Subsection (4) narrows standing to concrete, articulable legal injury, bars advisory opinions, and sets an organizational-standing rule requiring at least one member with standing and a germane organizational purpose — except where the Constitution expressly confers standing elsewhere. The same subsection forbids the Legislature from leaving any category of legal injury without a judicial forum, which prevents statutory drafting from quietly closing off access to court for an entire class of harm.

The jurisdictional provisions in (5) through (7) route specific, named categories of dispute to the Supreme Court rather than leaving them to percolate through the ordinary court structure: disputes between States or between a State and the Republic, domain disputes between the Legat Consul and Civic Consul under §2.14, challenges involving constitutionally independent institutions, emergency rights claims under §16.2, and amendment-consistency challenges under §17.3. Each of these categories involves either a structurally high-stakes conflict between constitutional actors or an independence protection that would make inferior-court review awkward, which is the stated basis for assigning them directly to the Supreme Court rather than running them through the ordinary appellate track. Subsection (6) adds expedited independent review for challenges to immediate defensive military authority during active operations; that review used to run through a fixed four-justice emergency panel, but that fixed panel conflicted with the Court's ordinary five-justice floor for constitutional questions, so the provision now gives the Supreme Court expedited jurisdiction and a bounded deadline while leaving the Court to set its own composition and procedure for that review. Subsection (7) preserves existing lawful operations during conflicts among constitutional actors, bars any actor from using refusal to certify, approve, or coordinate as a tool to suspend a constitutional obligation, and gives the Supreme Court expedited jurisdiction over such disputes — directly paralleling the Council of Ministers' own rule that disputed actions are suspended pending resolution while each Consul continues only functions clearly within their domain.

Subsection (8) addresses the risk of judicial delay itself: courts may issue interim protective orders to prevent irreparable harm, but a court's failure to rule within a prescribed period does not decide the merits or produce any substantive constitutional outcome, and the parties keep all otherwise available remedies. This closes off a particular abuse — using slow-walked litigation or missed deadlines to achieve a result a court never actually reached. Read together with the admissibility of NRS-published Monitor findings in (3) and the public-decision rule of the adjoining privacy provision, the section keeps judicial power bounded to adjudication on a public record, rather than policymaking, silent gatekeeping, or outcome-by-delay.

§4.5.a.text:
§4.5.a establishes a default of judicial transparency and then carves out a narrow, purpose-bound exception for personal privacy within that default. The opening sentence — "Judicial decisions are public" — makes publication the baseline rule for every ruling the courts issue, which is what lets §4.5(1) and §4.5(4) function as real checks: a court's power to void legislative or executive acts, or to resolve a concrete legal injury, only constrains other actors if the decision explaining that outcome is actually visible. This provision is the one place in Article IV that states the public-record rule for judicial output, so the privacy carve-out that follows has to operate as a bounded exception to that rule rather than a freestanding confidentiality power — consistent with keeping each protection in a single home rather than scattering partial disclosure rules across other judicial sections.

The operative design choice is the second sentence: courts "must protect personally identifying information where its disclosure is unnecessary to understand the decision, enforce the law, or preserve public accountability." The test is framed negatively — protection is required only where disclosure is *unnecessary* to those three named purposes — which means the default still favors disclosure whenever identifying information actually serves understanding the ruling, enforcing the law, or holding the system accountable. This is narrower than a blanket privacy shield: it doesn't let a court redact names simply because a party prefers anonymity, and it doesn't let a court withhold information that is itself needed to show how the law was applied or how the decision was reached. The provision names the holder of the duty (courts), the triggering condition (unnecessary disclosure of identifying information), and the standard courts must apply, satisfying the basic requirement that a constitutional duty identify who acts and under what condition.

Read against the rest of Article IV, this provision depends on the public-decision norm doing real work elsewhere: §4.5(3) makes Monitor findings published to the NRS admissible in judicial proceedings, and §4.2 and §4.1 establish the judges and courts whose rulings are the subject of §4.5.a's publication rule. The failure mode this guards against is a court using the general publicity of its decisions as a vehicle for exposing personal information that has no bearing on the legal reasoning, the enforcement of law, or public accountability for how justice was administered — for instance, publishing addresses, identifying details of victims or minors, or other incidental personal data that a bad-faith reading of "decisions are public" might otherwise sweep in. At the same time, by tying the privacy protection strictly to necessity, the provision guards against the opposite abuse: a court suppressing identifying details to shield itself, a litigant, or an official from accountability under the guise of privacy. The balance is enforced entirely through the necessity standard stated in the text itself, with no separate review mechanism specified in this provision for how that standard is applied.

§4.6.text:
§4.6 establishes full faith and credit across the Republic's constituent jurisdictions: a judgment, official record, or authenticated document valid in one State or Territory is recognized in all others. This is a structural guarantee of unity within a federated system — it treats the Republic's internal jurisdictions as parts of a single legal order rather than as separate sovereigns whose outputs require re-validation at every border. Without this baseline, a litigant could win a judgment in one jurisdiction only to find it treated as a foreign curiosity elsewhere, forcing relitigation and undermining the practical value of any judicial decision. The provision closes that gap by making recognition the default rule rather than a matter of discretion.

The design narrows the grounds for refusal to exactly two: the issuing court lacked jurisdiction, or the judgment was obtained by fraud. Naming only these two grounds forecloses a jurisdiction from refusing recognition for policy disagreement, procedural distaste, or hostility to the substance of the ruling — the kind of discretionary gatekeeping that would let a State nullify another's courts by relabeling disagreement as defect. The provision pairs this narrow carve-out with an explicit constitutional override: a judgment contrary to Article I is void under §17.4, which separately establishes that anything inconsistent with the Constitution is void to the extent of the inconsistency. This connects §4.6 to the Republic's supremacy clause rather than folding a constitutional-conflict rule into the jurisdiction/fraud exceptions — a judgment can be perfectly jurisdictionally sound and fraud-free and still be void if it conflicts with Article I's protections, because supremacy operates independently of ordinary recognition doctrine. The self-authentication mechanism for judgments or status orders published to the NRS works the same way: publication alone makes the record effective throughout the Republic without a separate re-registration step in each jurisdiction, eliminating the administrative friction and discretionary delay that a re-registration requirement would otherwise create. The anti-discrimination clause — barring a State or Territory from distinguishing recognition based on the parties or subject matter — closes the remaining gap: even where a jurisdiction cannot openly deny recognition, it could functionally undermine the obligation by selectively slow-walking or special-casing certain parties or subject matters.

The failure mode this provision guards against is a fragmented legal order in which jurisdictions use recognition as leverage — refusing or delaying enforcement of judgments involving disfavored litigants, subject matter, or outcomes — effectively letting local politics override adjudicated rights. By confining refusal to jurisdiction and fraud, voiding only for Article I conflicts under the Constitution's own supremacy rule, and making NRS publication self-executing and non-discriminatory in application, §4.6 keeps the recognition rule narrow, predictable, and resistant to case-by-case circumvention, while relying on §4.5's judicial review framework and §17.4's supremacy principle to handle the constitutional-conflict scenario rather than duplicating that function within the recognition rule itself.

§5.1.text:
§5.1 establishes citizenship itself as the gateway status for the Republic's entire political structure — it defines who is a citizen by birth, who may become one by naturalization, and under what narrow conditions that status can be taken away. The birthright rules combine three distinct bases: descent from a citizen parent, birth in the Republic to a legal-resident parent, and birth in the Republic to a stateless parent, with the last branch functioning as a backstop against creating a stateless child at the moment of birth. Full citizenship rights — voting and office eligibility — attach only at 18, separating the status of citizenship from the exercise of its political rights, a distinction the document relies on elsewhere since legal residents under §5.2 hold civil rights like work and contract capacity but not federal voting rights or office eligibility. Naturalization is left to statute for the residency period and qualifications, with honorable military or national service shortening that period, but every pathway is funneled through a single mandatory checkpoint: the civic and constitutional proficiency assessment defined in §5.1.b. That assessment is administered by an independent agency under §3.9 and is barred from evaluating political opinion or cultural loyalty, which keeps the gate to citizenship a test of civic knowledge rather than a tool for screening applicants by belief or background.

The revocation rules in §5.1 were tightened to correct a specific structural weakness. The provision once protected natural-born citizens absolutely while protecting naturalized citizens only by a ban on revocation "as punishment" — a qualifier that depends on the revoking government's own characterization of its act, the same flaw already identified in another provision's redistricting language where a limit rested on the actor's self-description rather than on anything observable. The current text replaces that weak qualifier with an objective judicial standard: naturalized citizenship may be revoked only by judicial finding, on clear and convincing evidence, that it was obtained through material fraud in the application. That change also closed a second gap — the document previously left unaddressed the one case where revocation is genuinely defensible, namely fraud in the naturalization process itself — while adding two further limits: revocation can never be used where it would cause statelessness, and it never reaches back to strip derivative citizenship already acquired by someone else through that person. Citizenship as punishment is barred outright, for anyone.

The final rule addresses a child who joins a parent after that parent already obtained residency or citizenship: the child receives the parent's status as of the joining date, provided the child arrives within a statutory window that cannot be set below five years. This protects family unity for children whose arrival lagged a parent's own status change, without allowing statute to shrink that protection below a fixed floor. Together, these mechanisms guard against statelessness at birth, against naturalization standards that discriminate on belief rather than knowledge, against citizenship stripping used as a political or punitive weapon disguised as an administrative act, and against a child's delayed arrival erasing the benefit of a parent's already-settled status.

§5.1.a.text:
The constitution treats voting citizenship as a geographic fact that must attach to exactly one State or Territory, never two and never none. Before this provision existed, the document defined federal citizenship in §5.1 and required voter eligibility to be checked against citizenship and residency records, but nothing settled what those records were supposed to establish about *which* State or Territory a citizen belonged to. That gap mattered practically because petition mechanisms elsewhere in the constitution depend on counting "eligible voters within" a defined geographic area, and no rule existed for assigning a citizen to one such area rather than another, or for preventing a citizen from counting in two at once or in none. §5.1.a closes that gap by setting a floor and a ceiling simultaneously: every citizen is a voting citizen of exactly one State or Territory, determined by residence or domicile under applicable law, and no law may leave a citizen without one.

The operative mechanism is the conflict rule in the final sentence: statute must resolve conflicting claims, and recognition in one jurisdiction automatically terminates prior recognition in another. This means the provision does not depend on an administrative revocation process to keep a citizen's voting-citizenship singular — the act of a new jurisdiction recognizing someone as its voting citizen is itself what ends the old recognition, as a matter of constitutional rule rather than bureaucratic action. The practical effect is that the question "which jurisdiction counts this person's vote" is never left open-ended or dependent on discretionary choice; the legislature is directed to build the statutory machinery for resolving competing claims (for example, where someone's residence and domicile point to different places), but the constitutional default already guarantees that whatever the statute decides, the result is one jurisdiction, not a tie and not a gap.

This provision sits beneath §5.1, which creates citizenship itself and fixes the age — 18 — at which a citizen acquires full citizenship rights including voting. §5.1.a does not decide who is a citizen or when their voting rights begin; it operates only once that status exists, answering a separate question of geographic assignment. It also sits against §5.2, which confirms that legal residents, unlike citizens, hold no federal voting rights at all — underscoring that §5.1.a's assignment problem belongs only to citizens, since residents are not in the pool of voting citizens to be located in the first place. The failure mode this provision guards against is the one identified directly: without a settled rule, a citizen could be double-counted across two jurisdictions' voter rolls, inflating the "eligible voters within" figures that geographic petition thresholds rely on, or could fall through the cracks and be counted nowhere, effectively disenfranchised by jurisdictional ambiguity rather than by any lawful restriction. By making singularity and non-exclusion a constitutional floor rather than a statutory option, the provision prevents a legislature from ever writing residency rules that produce either outcome, even inadvertently.

§5.1.b.text:
§5.1.b establishes the civic and constitutional proficiency assessment that every naturalization applicant must pass, and it answers a structural question that naturalization raises: who decides what a prospective citizen needs to know, and how is that decision kept from becoming a tool of political screening. The provision embodies the Democratic Legitimacy Test — the gate into citizenship must rest on a pre-political standard, not on a policy preference held by whichever government happens to be in power when an applicant applies. It accomplishes this by fixing three things in the constitutional text itself: the assessment must exist ("the Republic must maintain" it), it must be run by an independent agency rather than by an executive department, and it is barred from evaluating political opinion or cultural loyalty. Everything else — the actual test content, question format, scoring, and administration procedure — is left to statute, which is the ordinary mechanism for filling in operational detail once the constitutional floor is set.

The design choice to house the assessment inside an independent agency rather than a ministry or the naturalization office itself draws on §3.9, which governs independent statutory agencies. Under §3.9, such an agency sits outside either executive's authority, its leadership holds fixed terms removable only for conduct, incapacity, or incompetence, and its qualification requirements may not be written to exclude people for their political or policy views. Placing the assessment under that structure means the body writing and grading citizenship questions cannot be reshuffled or pressured by a sitting executive for short-term political advantage, and the Legislature that created the agency may alter or abolish it only through ordinary statute, not by quietly stripping its independence. The explicit tie to §1.6 layers on a second constraint: the assessment, as a government action, is bound by the equality and non-discrimination floor, so its administration cannot draw distinctions on listed characteristics like national origin or religion without compelling justification. The Legat Consul's naturalization reference in §5.1 confirms the dependency runs the other way too — every naturalization pathway requires passing the assessment §5.1.b establishes, so this provision is the single place that civic knowledge requirement lives, consistent with keeping each protection in one place rather than scattering testing standards across multiple citizenship provisions.

The specific exclusion of political opinion and cultural loyalty from the assessment's scope targets a concrete failure mode: a knowledge test is an easy vehicle for ideological screening if left unconstrained, since "proficiency" could silently expand to cover approved opinions or cultural conformity rather than factual civic and constitutional knowledge. By naming that boundary directly in the constitutional text, the provision prevents statute from redefining the test's purpose later, even though statute retains full control over content and administration within that boundary. The independent-agency placement guards a related risk — that whichever political faction controls naturalization policy could tighten or loosen the test to admit or exclude applicants by political calculation rather than by applying a stable, knowledge-based standard administered at arm's length from executive control.

§5.2.text:
§5.2 draws the line between civic status and civic membership: it defines what a legal resident can do economically and socially within the Republic, and what they cannot do politically. Legal residents may work, enter contracts, own property, and access the social-state systems under Article XII — a substantial bundle of rights tied to lawful presence and participation in the economy and the welfare system, independent of citizenship. But the same sentence structure that grants that bundle also withholds two specific things: federal voting rights and eligibility for federal office. This is a status provision, not a rights-creation provision in the open-ended sense — it enumerates a fixed set of entitlements and a fixed pair of exclusions, with no residual category implied either way.

The design choice here is to separate economic and civil participation from federal political power, and to do that separation at the level of federal voting and federal office specifically — not all public life. This connects directly to §5.1, the citizenship provision, which states that citizens acquire full citizenship rights, including voting and eligibility for office, at 18, and that a legal resident may earn citizenship upon meeting the legal qualifications and continuous residency period established by statute. Read together, §5.1 and §5.2 create a two-tier structure: legal residency confers a defined civil and economic status immediately, while federal political rights are reserved for citizenship and attained through a statutory naturalization pathway rather than through residency alone. The exclusion in §5.2 is therefore not a permanent bar on legal residents as people — it is a statement that this particular status, as such, does not carry federal voting or federal office eligibility; those are acquired by crossing into citizenship under the separate pathway §5.1 defines.

Structurally, this keeps the citizenship/voting boundary in one place. §5.1 is where the acquisition of full political rights is defined and tied to age and naturalization; §5.2 does not re-grant or re-restrict those rights, it simply confirms that legal-resident status does not include them. That avoids duplicating or contradicting the voting-eligibility rule in two separate provisions. The failure mode this guards against is the conflation of lawful presence with full political membership — allowing someone to claim federal voting rights or federal office eligibility merely from working, contracting, owning property, or receiving social-state benefits as a legal resident, without having gone through the naturalization qualifications and residency period §5.1 requires. By listing the civil and economic entitlements legal residents hold and then explicitly denying the two federal political entitlements in the same breath, §5.2 forecloses any argument that the broad grant of economic and social participation implicitly extends to the franchise or to federal office.

§5.3.text:
§5.3 sits inside Article V's structure of citizenship and status, but it does something different from §5.1 and §5.2: those provisions define who holds citizen or legal-resident status, while §5.3 protects a child's custodial stability regardless of which status applies. The provision embodies a pre-political protection — a child's dependency on a primary caregiver is not a policy choice subject to ordinary immigration or enforcement discretion, but a structural fact the Republic must account for whenever it removes a parent or guardian. The mechanism is preventive, not remedial: when removing a parent or guardian "would deprive a child of their primary caregiver," the Republic must ensure care, housing, and connection to remaining family, and — critically — the removal order itself is stayed until custodial arrangements are resolved. The stay operates on the timing of removal, stopping the separation from happening at all while custody is worked out, rather than compensating for a separation already completed. This distinguishes the provision from a scheme that merely promises post-removal services; the order cannot execute until the child's custodial situation is addressed, which is the provision's central design choice.

The second sentence adds a distinct, narrower rule: no child of a citizen or legal resident may be deported because of the child's own documentation status. This clause is actor-specific and status-specific — it protects children whose parent holds citizen or legal-resident status, addressing the particular failure mode where a child could otherwise be removed on the theory that the child personally lacks documentation, even though the parent's status under §5.1 or §5.2 would otherwise anchor the family in the Republic. This is a separate guarantee from the stay in the first sentence: the stay is triggered by the removal of a caregiver and concerns timing and custodial resolution, while the deportation bar is triggered by the child's own documentation status and concerns removability outright. Reading them together, §5.3 closes two different gaps — one where a parent's removal threatens to leave a child without care, and one where a child's own paperwork is used as the pretext for removal despite a parent's established status.

The provision depends on Article V's status definitions to make sense of its terms: §5.1 establishes how a child becomes a citizen from birth, and §5.2 defines legal residents as those who may work, hold property, and access social-state systems but lack federal voting rights. §5.3's second sentence borrows directly from these categories — "citizen or legal resident" — to mark which parents' status triggers the deportation bar for their children. The provision's internal consistency was itself a point of correction: the stay clause was revised because its subject once shifted silently to cover only non-citizen children while the provision's opening sentences addressed citizen children, an inversion inconsistent with a remedial-then-preventive structure covering all children regardless of status. The failure mode §5.3 guards against is the use of a parent's removal, or a child's own paperwork, as a mechanism to inflict family separation or statelessness-like disruption on a child who had no role in creating the status question — treating the child as incidental to an enforcement action against the adult, rather than as someone whose caregiving relationship the Republic must affirmatively preserve.

§6.1.text:
§6.1 establishes immigration as a two-stage process — State or federal sponsorship followed by federal certification — and the structure itself is the constitutional safeguard: no single actor controls the full path to legal residency. Sponsorship identifies who may apply, certification determines who is actually admitted, and the two functions are kept institutionally distinct. States retain real discretion over whom they sponsor, but that discretion is bounded by §1.6, which bars discrimination on listed characteristics absent compelling justification and requires other distinctions to be rationally related to a legitimate governmental purpose. This prevents a State from using sponsorship as a backdoor for the kind of exclusion the equality provision forbids, while still letting States exercise a genuine policy role in selecting sponsees. Federal certification categories, by contrast, are set by statute, and the provision adds an explicit substantive floor at that stage — and indeed at any stage — barring ideological screening and nationality-based quotas. That dual bar closes off the two most historically familiar routes to pretextual exclusion: a State using sponsorship criteria that functionally discriminate, and the federal certifying authority using category design to achieve the same result from the other direction.

The written-denial requirement and the automatic vesting rule work together as the provision's enforcement logic against stalling or hidden rejection. Any denial must specify the precise ground in writing, which prevents either level of government from rejecting an applicant without an articulable, recorded reason — a structural check against arbitrary or disguised discriminatory denial, since a vague or unstated ground cannot satisfy the requirement. Then, once both stages are actually completed, residency vests by operation of law, and neither executive may delay, condition, or deny that status. This closes the specific failure mode of an executive sitting on a technically-completed application indefinitely or attaching informal conditions after the fact: completion of the two stages is self-executing, not subject to further executive discretion. The aggregate-limits power given to the Legislature operates at a different level entirely — it caps total volume over a period rather than individual eligibility — so a legislature can manage overall flow without being able to use volume caps to defeat an individual's completed claim to status.

Asylum under §1.17 and Territorial immigration are carved out as separate tracks rather than folded into the two-stage system. Asylum claims are exempt from ordinary sponsorship, certification, and aggregate limits, and no refusal of sponsorship may extinguish such a claim — meaning a person's asylum right survives independently of whether any State or federal sponsor accepted them, keeping the asylum pathway (determined under §6.3) analytically separate from the sponsorship-driven ordinary system so that aggregate caps or sponsorship denials can never be used to choke off asylum access. Territories sit outside the sponsorship/certification framework as well: immigration there runs under federal standards, with each Territory negotiating volumes and qualifications through its Territorial Compact, the instrument that in each case also guarantees the Territory an elected local governing authority over local matters — reflecting that Territorial immigration is a negotiated, compact-based arrangement rather than a State-sponsorship relationship.

§6.2.text:
§6.2 sits at the enforcement end of the Republic's immigration framework, and its first rule is the most structurally important: only the federal government may remove a person from the Republic. This centralizes a specific coercive power — physical removal — in a single actor, which prevents States, localities, or private parties from exercising what is in effect banishment authority. Because Article VI's two-stage system involves State sponsorship as one track and federal certification as another, this clause makes clear that whatever role States play in sponsorship decisions, they have no independent power to expel anyone. The consequence of this allocation is that removal is a federal act or it does not happen at all; there is no parallel State enforcement track to police.

Subsection (2) builds an appeals structure directly onto the two-stage system named elsewhere in the Article. State sponsorship denials can be challenged specifically on discrimination grounds under §1.6, which requires compelling justification for distinctions based on listed characteristics like race, religion, or national origin, and rational relation to a legitimate purpose for other distinctions. Federal certification denials made on national security grounds instead go through judicial review, with courts determining the appropriate remedy. This is a deliberate two-track appeal structure keyed to the two-track immigration system itself: the ground of challenge differs depending on which stage denied the person status, and the text does not create a single unified appeal standard across both tracks. Courts are left to fashion remedy rather than the provision specifying one, which keeps the remedy flexible to the type of denial involved. An earlier editorial pass removed a reference to "four certified categories" from this provision once the certification framework in §6.1 was updated, replacing it with the current language pointing to "federal certification mandate" — a stale-reference fix rather than a substantive rewrite of the appeals mechanism.

Subsection (3) extends appointed counsel at public expense to anyone subject to removal proceedings or challenging a decision under this section, conditioned on inability to afford representation. This guarantees that the right of appeal created in subsection (2) is not merely formal — a person facing State sponsorship denial or federal certification denial has a lawyer available to mount the discrimination or judicial-review challenge regardless of means. The same appointed-counsel guarantee appears in the asylum proceedings described elsewhere in the Article, extending representation to applicants who cannot afford it, so the pattern of publicly funded counsel for people facing loss of status or removal recurs across the Article's two major procedural contexts rather than being unique to §6.2. Without the counsel guarantee, the appeal rights in subsection (2) would be available in form but inaccessible in practice to anyone lacking resources to litigate against the federal government's certification or a State's sponsorship denial, which is the failure mode this subsection closes off.

§6.3.text:
§6.3 sets the structural guarantee that stands behind non-refoulement: a person cannot actually be protected from return to danger unless someone determines whether they qualify for asylum before removal happens, and unless that determination follows a procedure resistant to manipulation by the removing authority itself. Subsection (1) makes this concrete with a timing rule rather than a vague standard — a claim "must be determined before removal may be executed," so the government cannot moot the protection by acting first and litigating later. Subsection (2) reinforces this by making residency flow automatically from a federal court's asylum grant: no State sponsorship, no federal certification, nothing else to withhold or delay. This is a deliberate departure from the ordinary immigration architecture of §6.1 and §6.2, where State sponsorship and federal certification are the normal gatekeeping mechanisms — asylum bypasses both, because a court's determination of persecution risk is the only legitimate basis for the outcome. Subsection (3) closes an obvious evasion: a government that cannot refuse asylum outright might instead punish irregular entry as a proxy, so penalties "arising solely from irregular entry" are barred for anyone with a pending or granted claim.

Subsection (5) assigns adjudication to "independent courts within the judicial branch," which is the Institution Test at work — asylum determinations use the existing judicial structure rather than a new immigration tribunal, and independence matters because an adjudicator housed inside the enforcement apparatus would face an obvious incentive to defer to removal goals. The Legislature's role is deliberately narrow: under §3.1 it is the body that "provide[s] for their jurisdiction and proceedings by statute," meaning it builds the structural plumbing but does not touch the merits. Subsection (4) then specifies what that statute must guarantee regardless of its other content: a qualified adjudicator, interpreter access, evidence and witness rights, appointed counsel where the applicant cannot afford one, a written decision with grounds, and appeal — plus accessibility for Territories and remote areas, so geography cannot function as a backdoor denial of process. Appointed counsel here tracks the same actor-and-consequence logic as §6.2(3)'s removal-proceeding counsel right, giving asylum seekers a procedural floor comparable to other immigration litigants rather than a lesser one.

Subsections (6) and (7) extend the provision's protective logic to the person least able to invoke it alone: an unaccompanied minor. The minor holds full §1.18 non-refoulement protection "from the moment of contact," and a federal court with jurisdiction over that point of contact must appoint a guardian within 72 hours — a hard deadline that forecloses indefinite limbo for a child with no one to act on their behalf. Detention is permitted only where "lawful and necessary" and only in a facility "specifically designated and resourced for children," foreclosing the use of general detention infrastructure as a default. Read together with §6.3.a, which keeps a person at liberty, subject to ordinary law, when removal cannot be executed, the provision's overall effect is to prevent the enforcement system from using delay, geography, cost, or a child's incapacity as tools to defeat a protection that §1.18 already promises in substance.

§6.3.a.text:
§6.3.a addresses a narrow but concrete gap in the removal process: what happens to a person when a removal order exists but cannot actually be carried out. Rather than leaving such a person in an undefined limbo — neither removed nor formally status-holding — the provision fixes their condition by operation of constitutional text: they remain at liberty, and they remain subject to all applicable laws of the jurisdiction where they reside. This is a status-default provision. It does not grant residency, asylum, or any affirmative immigration status; it simply forecloses indefinite detention or extralegal limbo as the consequence of an order the government cannot execute, while making clear that ordinary law continues to apply to the person exactly as it would to anyone else in that jurisdiction.

The design choice here is to resolve the unexecutable-order scenario with a liberty default rather than silence or administrative discretion. The practical effect is that the inability to execute a removal order does not itself become a lawful basis for continued detention or for placing the person outside the protection of ordinary law. The provision pairs that liberty with an explicit subjection to "all applicable laws of the jurisdiction in which they reside" — meaning the person is not granted any special immunity or elevated status by virtue of the order's failure; they simply fall back into the ordinary legal order governing everyone else there. This sits within §6.3's broader architecture of fixing status outcomes for people caught in incomplete or stalled government action: §6.3(2) does the analogous work for a granted asylum claim, converting a court's determination directly into legal residency "by operation of that determination," without requiring further sponsorship or certification steps. §6.3.a performs a structurally similar function for the opposite case — a removal order that stalls — by converting the stalled state into a defined, if minimal, status (liberty subject to law) rather than leaving it undetermined.

The provision depends on §6.2's framework for how removal orders arise in the first place, since only the federal government may remove a person under §6.2(1), and it is that same removal authority whose order may go unexecuted. It also sits logically downstream of §6.3(1), which requires that any asylum claim be determined before removal may be executed — meaning a removal order's unexecutability could stem from a pending claim, a practical obstacle, or another barrier, and §6.3.a supplies the default status regardless of which.
