Finally, the provision specifies that incapacity or suspension does not vacate the permanent office or interrupt its term — the term keeps running on the original officeholder's clock even while someone else exercises the authority. This distinguishes a temporary gap from a true vacancy: the permanent seat and its ten-year non-renewable term, fixed in §9.1, stay intact, and the Acting Monitor General's tenure is bounded by the earlier of a permanent successor assuming office or the original Monitor General's authority being restored. Without this provision, a term's end or an incapacity could either freeze a Monitor's audit function entirely or let an acting officer entrench themselves, either of which would expose the audit function to exactly the kind of capture the selection rules for permanent Monitor Generals were built to prevent.

§9.1.e.text:
This provision gives the Republic a way to handle a Monitor General who cannot function without treating incapacity as a backdoor removal. Each Monitor General holds a 10-year non-renewable term under §9.1, and that term is meant to run its course undisturbed by shifting political winds. Incapacity, by contrast, is a functional reality that can strike without warning, and the office needs a mechanism distinct from removal to cover it. The provision supplies two tracks: self-declaration by the Monitor General, and, where the officer is unable to declare it themselves, a determination by the same authority responsible for suspension under §9.7.a. That second track is bounded tightly — it must rest on stated functional grounds, and political or policy disagreement alone does not qualify. This guards against the obvious abuse risk named by the Bad-Faith Test: a body uncomfortable with a Monitor General's findings could otherwise relabel disagreement as incapacity to sideline an inconvenient officer without going through removal.

The mechanism connects directly to the Acting Monitor General structure in §9.1.d, which assumes authority during the incapacity period, and to the suspension authority in §9.7.a, which supplies the actor empowered to make an involuntary determination. Critically, incapacity does not vacate the office or interrupt the term — the incumbent remains the Monitor General in a legal sense, distinguishing this from the permanent removal process under §9.9. The text makes that boundary explicit: temporary incapacity may not be used as a substitute for permanent removal. This keeps the two tracks from collapsing into each other — removal requires whatever separate process §9.9 establishes, while incapacity is a stopgap for functional inability, not a judgment on fitness for office.

The recovery and review mechanics protect the officer against indefinite or pretextual restriction. The affected Monitor General may declare recovery and resume authority immediately, and that default favors restoration — the burden sits on the authority that imposed an involuntary determination to go to court and obtain judicial relief preventing restoration, and that authority must establish grounds for continuing the restriction. Pairing this with expedited independent judicial review gives the self-declaration default real teeth: a suspending authority cannot simply sit on an incapacity finding and let it persist by default, since inaction effectively returns authority to the incumbent. The publication requirement for involuntary grounds also ties into the Monitors' general transparency practice, such as the duty to publish reasons when an investigation is discontinued, while expressly carving out confidential personal information from what must be disclosed — balancing public accountability for the suspending authority's action against the Monitor General's personal privacy.

§9.2.text:
§9.2 states a single structural rule that governs how all three Monitors General come into office: whoever selects a Monitor cannot be the institution that Monitor is supposed to watch. This is the independence principle underlying the entire Monitor system — oversight only functions if the watcher is not a creature of the watched. The provision itself is spare; it does not name the selecting bodies or describe lotteries, nominations, or confirmations. It states the exclusion rule as a constraint that any selection process must satisfy, leaving the actual mechanics — who nominates, who confirms, what happens on failure — to §9.3. That separation of principle from mechanism means §9.2 is the test a selection design must pass, while §9.3 is the design that passes it: the Supreme Court nominates the Legislative Monitor General, the Assembly and Senate Speakers jointly nominate the Executive Monitor General, and the Judicial Monitor General is drawn by public lottery from a candidate pool, with all three confirmed by national popular vote. None of these selecting actors is the body each respective Monitor is charged with auditing, which is exactly what §9.2 demands.

The structural history behind this provision frames it as the foundation on which the whole Monitor architecture rests: selection was insulated so that no audited institution controls who becomes its auditor. That same history notes that removal, by contrast, was not originally insulated in the same way — under a prior version of §9.9, removal of any Monitor General ran through the Supreme Court and a two-thirds vote of both chambers, which for the Judicial Monitor General meant the audited judiciary had a gatekeeping role over removing its own auditor. That contrast is instructive for reading §9.2 narrowly: the exclusion rule it states governs selection, not removal, discipline, or any other interaction between a Monitor and the institution it oversees. Expanding §9.2 to cover removal would exceed what its text says, even though the same independence logic plainly motivated later attention to removal design.

§9.2 also underwrites why the oversight architecture is given heightened amendment protection: the core Monitor provisions, including §9.2, were later made subject to Popular Ratification rather than State Ratification alone, so that the branches being checked cannot alter the independence rule that checks them through an easier amendment path. This reflects the same logic the selection rule itself encodes — an oversight mechanism is only as strong as the political actors' inability to capture or dilute it, whether by controlling selection in the first instance or by amending the rule that prevents such control. The failure mode §9.2 guards against is capture at the point of appointment: if the Legislative branch could select its own Monitor, or the Executive could pick its own, the oversight function would become nominal, since an auditor chosen by the audited has every incentive to go easy on its patron. By fixing the exclusion as a standing constraint on selection design, §9.2 forecloses that outcome regardless of how §9.3's specific nomination and confirmation procedures are later amended by statute, so long as any such amendment still keeps the audited institution out of the selection chain.

§9.3.text:
§9.3 governs how all three Monitors General — Legislative, Executive, and Judicial — reach office, and it embodies the constitutional principle that the three Monitor offices, despite checking different branches, should be filled through parallel, publicly accountable procedures rather than divergent ones. Every confirmation, regardless of which body nominates the candidate, ends the same way: a national popular vote at the next federal electoral period by simple majority, administered uniformly by the Elections Panel, with timing set by statute to ensure seamless succession. This shared final stage reflects Procedural Familiarity — the nomination paths differ, but the legitimating step does not. If a confirmation vote fails, §9.1.d's acting mechanism takes over and a new selection must begin within 60 days, which prevents a failed vote from creating an indefinite vacancy and ties §9.3 directly to §9.1.d's acting-officer machinery rather than inventing a separate interim rule.

The nomination paths themselves are deliberately differentiated by actor while converging on the same lottery-based fallback. The LM Monitor General is nominated by the SC from the LM candidate pool, audited jointly by the EM and JM; if the SC misses the 60-day window, the JMC must select by public lottery from that pool. The EM Monitor General is nominated jointly by the Assembly Speaker and Senate Speaker from the EM pool, audited jointly by the LM and JM, with JM disclosure-audit findings published to the NRS before the vote — a transparency step satisfying the Transparency and Sunlight Tests by putting the nominee's disclosure record on record before the public votes. If the Speakers fail to jointly nominate within 60 days, the JMC again lottery-selects. The JM Monitor General skips nomination entirely and is chosen by public lottery under §9.8 from the pool defined in §9.4. Each path's cross-branch auditing (EM/JM auditing the LM pool, LM/JM auditing the EM pool) guards against a Monitor's own branch controlling who polices it, while the uniform 60-day lottery fallback prevents any nominating actor from stalling a vacancy indefinitely by simply not nominating.

The 18-month spacing rule — barring two Monitor General full terms from being scheduled to begin within 18 months of each other, with remainder-of-term service not counting as a new term for this purpose — guards against simultaneous turnover across all three oversight offices, which would otherwise leave the system without experienced Monitors at once. The one-time-service rule closes a related gap: anyone confirmed to a full term may not re-enter any Monitor General pool, and anyone confirmed to serve a remainder-of-term following an unscheduled vacancy may not re-enter the pool for that same capacity, though they remain eligible for the other two capacities. This mirrors the single-tenure logic applied elsewhere to judicial pool crossover, closing the parallel gap where a person might otherwise cycle through repeated Monitor service. Acting service under §9.1.d is expressly excluded from counting as confirmation, keeping temporary stand-in service from triggering these eligibility locks, and successors assume full authority either at the precise moment a scheduled term ends or immediately upon certification following an unscheduled vacancy, which fixes the transfer-of-authority instant without any gap in coverage.

§9.4.text:
§9.4 defines who may enter the Judicial Monitor Candidate Pool, the body of former judges eligible to serve as Judicial Monitor, and assigns that pool's audit function jointly to the Legislative and Executive Monitors. The eligibility rule restricts entry to former State or Republic judges who sat on a court of record at trial level or above, with a one-year cooling-off period after leaving judicial office. Former Supreme Court justices face a longer five-year cooling-off period before they may enter this pool. This tiered waiting period structurally reflects the greater institutional weight and visibility of Supreme Court service: a justice who sat on the court defined in §4.3, serving a single non-renewable 12-year term, carries more residual influence, relationships, and reputational entanglement with the judiciary than a trial-level judge, so a longer separation is required before that person can be considered to audit and oversee courts as Judicial Monitor.

The pool's eligibility criteria and its audit arrangement connect directly to §9.1.c, which defines the Judicial Monitor as the officer who audits the courts, judicial officers, the Elections Panel, and treaty/compact compliance. Because the Judicial Monitor is drawn from this candidate pool, the composition rules here determine who can eventually hold that auditing authority — former judges with substantial court-of-record experience and sufficient distance from active judicial service. The joint audit of the pool itself by the Legislative and Executive Monitors is a check performed by the other two Monitors rather than by the judiciary or by the Judicial Monitor's own pool, keeping oversight of candidate eligibility outside the institution those candidates will eventually audit. This separation is reinforced by the broader three-Monitor structure in Article IX, where each Monitor is checked by the other two rather than self-policing.

The cooling-off periods guard against a former judge, and especially a former Supreme Court justice, moving directly from the bench into a role auditing the very institution and colleagues they recently served with, which could compromise independence or create the appearance of continued judicial loyalty overriding audit rigor. The heading of this provision was corrected from language describing a certification mandate to language describing an audit mandate, reflecting that the Judicial Monitor no longer certifies individual applicants to pools or registries on a per-applicant basis; that certification function was removed as part of a broader shift in how Monitor audit authority operates, leaving the Elections Panel to apply eligibility criteria while the Monitors audit that administration rather than performing certification themselves. The joint Legislative-Executive audit of this particular pool follows that same pattern: it monitors the Elections Panel's application of the §9.4(1) criteria rather than substituting for it, and the one- and five-year thresholds set the substantive boundary that audit is checking.

§9.4.a.text:
§9.4.a sets the entry gate for the single pool from which every federal judicial appointment is drawn, and it embodies the constitutional principle that judicial eligibility must rest on pre-political, professional qualifications rather than discretionary appointment by another branch. The design choice is direct application: any citizen meeting the threshold — 15 years of legal practice or 10 years of judicial service, plus no disqualifying financial interest under §7.10 — may apply straight to the Elections Panel. There is no nominating gatekeeper screening candidates into the pool; the Panel applies the criteria, and Monitors audit that administration rather than certifying individual applicants, which keeps the eligibility determination mechanical and auditable rather than a matter of institutional favor. Temporary or acting judicial service does not count toward the 10-year judicial-service threshold, which closes an obvious path to inflating qualifications through short-term or non-permanent postings.

The provision's repeat-use rules are calibrated by tier rather than applied as one blanket bar. A former Supreme Court justice may never re-enter the Judicial Pool — once someone has sat on the Court, that door is permanently closed. For every other federal judicial appointment, the bar is narrower: a person who has served in one such appointment cannot be nominated again to that same court, but remains eligible for nomination to a different federal court. This structure replaced an earlier version that barred anyone confirmed to any federal judicial appointment from ever being nominated to another. That broader rule proved to work against the quality of the bench: it treated ordinary career progression — district court to appellate court to Supreme Court — as if it were an attempt to hoard scarce seats, and it created a perverse incentive for ambitious candidates to decline a district appointment altogether rather than foreclose a later Supreme Court nomination. The current text separates the two concerns: same-court repetition is barred to prevent entrenchment in a single seat, while cross-court movement is preserved so the bench can draw its highest court from candidates with real judicial experience rather than filtering them out.

The provision depends on §7.10's definition of a disqualifying financial interest — one creating a direct and material conflict with impartial exercise of official duties — to give content to the "no disqualifying financial interest" criterion, and it supplies judicial appointments under Article IV with their only source pool, since all federal judicial appointments are drawn from it. It sits beside, but is structurally distinct from, the Judicial Monitor Candidate Pool described in the same article, which draws on former State or Republic judges under separate cooling-off terms; the two pools serve different appointment tracks and are not interchangeable. The failure mode this provision guards against is twofold: unqualified or conflicted individuals reaching the federal bench absent a professional-experience and financial-integrity floor, and a seat-hoarding dynamic in which repeated appointment to the same court entrenches incumbents or discourages experienced judges from taking the assignments the system most needs filled.

§9.5.text:
§9.5 establishes how a Monitor's work reaches the public once it exists, and the design logic is that oversight only functions if its findings cannot be intercepted on the way out. The provision embodies the Transparency Test directly: Monitor findings and assessments "must be published permanently to the NRS," with the only carve-outs being constitutional protections for confidential information and lawful security interests — narrow, named exceptions rather than open-ended discretion. The structural guarantee that makes this work is the line that "no authority outside the issuing Monitor may suppress, delay, alter, or classify its findings." That single sentence is doing the real work of the Institutional Power Test: it locates the power to decide what gets published in the Monitor itself, and forecloses the most obvious failure mode — a reviewed institution, or any outside actor, quietly editing or sitting on an inconvenient finding before it reaches the NRS. The access clause reinforces the same logic from the input side: Monitors get "unrestricted access to records, personnel, facilities, and systems" within their mandates, but that access is explicitly not a license to disclose confidential or classified material publicly, keeping the confidentiality boundary consistent whether the question is what a Monitor may see or what a Monitor may publish.

The second paragraph extends the publication guarantee to the people actually doing the work. Monitor personnel may independently disclose evidence of improper suppression or alteration of findings to the NRS, under the same confidentiality protections that bound the findings themselves, and must be protected from retaliation for making a lawful disclosure. This closes a gap the first paragraph alone would leave open: barring outside suppression is not enough if someone could still quietly pressure or punish the staff who noticed it. By giving individual personnel their own disclosure channel and shielding them from retaliation, the provision makes the no-suppression rule self-reinforcing rather than dependent on the Monitor's own leadership catching every instance of interference. The obstruction clause performs a parallel function for the access guarantee: obstruction of a Monitor acting within its constitutional mandate "must be documented and published to the NRS," turning interference into a visible, permanent record rather than something that can be absorbed quietly inside the obstructing institution.

The joint State of the Republic report is a separate mechanic layered on top of the ongoing publication duty — a periodic, combined account from all three Monitors to the Legislature and the citizens, rather than another findings-publication event. Within the article, §9.5.a and §9.5.b show the next steps in the pipeline: findings go to the institution responsible for the matter, that institution makes any compliance determination, a subject body must respond on the NRS within a statutory period, and none of this substitutes for that body's own constitutional duties. §9.5 itself stops short of those downstream steps — it governs only how findings get out and stay unaltered, not what happens to them afterward. The practical effect of keeping those functions separate is that the publication guarantee cannot be weakened by arguments about compliance procedure, and the compliance procedure cannot be used as a backdoor to delay or dilute what the Monitor said.

§9.5.a.text:
§9.5.a sits at the point where a Monitor's information-only observation meets a constitutional actor's obligation to act on it, and it is built to keep those two roles from collapsing into one. The provision has three operative pieces. First, Monitors must publish their audit findings to the NRS and also submit them to the constitutional institution responsible for the matter under review — a dual channel that makes the finding public record while also routing it to whichever body actually has jurisdiction over the underlying conduct. Second, where the Constitution requires a compliance determination based on an audit, the responsible institution — not the Monitor — makes that determination, and it does so under whatever constitutional and statutory procedures already govern that institution's own decisions. Third, a body or officer subject to a Monitor report must publish a response to the NRS within a period set by statute, but that response need not agree with the Monitor's findings.

This structure depends directly on §9.1's definition of what a Monitor is: an information-only mandate that observes, assesses, and publishes, with findings that are not binding on any constitutional actor and not a prerequisite for any legal proceeding or governmental function except where the Constitution expressly attaches a consequence to one. §9.5.a is the mechanism that operationalizes that limit — it tells you what happens to a finding once it leaves the Monitor's hands, and it assigns the actual determination of compliance to the institution with jurisdiction, under that institution's own procedures, rather than to the Monitor itself. §9.5.b reinforces the same boundary from the other direction, stating that Monitor findings do not substitute for a responsible body's independent obligation to perform its own duties. Read together, the two provisions keep the Monitor as an observer and publisher of record while leaving the institution answerable for the decision and the body under review answerable for a public reply.

The failure mode this guards against is the quiet absorption of enforcement power into an office that was only ever given the power to observe and publish. If a Monitor's finding could itself constitute or force a compliance determination, or if a body under review could simply absorb a finding into silence, the information-only character of the Monitor role would erode in practice even though it remains untouched on paper. The mandatory NRS response requirement forecloses silent non-response: the subject body must put something on the public record within the statutory period, even if that something is disagreement. The determination is left with the institution that already holds procedural authority over the matter — consistent with using existing constitutional bodies rather than letting the Monitor's audit function double as an adjudicative one — while the publication and submission duties guarantee that the finding cannot be buried before the responsible institution ever sees it or before the public can see what was found and how the subject answered.

§9.5.b.text:
§9.5.b draws a clean line between two kinds of constitutional authority that could otherwise be confused: the Monitor's power to find facts and publish them, and the responsible body's power to act on them. The provision states flatly that monitor findings, reports, and assessments do not substitute for a responsible body's independent obligation to perform its constitutional and statutory duties or to act on matters within its operational authority. This is an informational-power boundary — the Monitor system is built entirely on fact-finding, publication, and audit (as §9.5 and §9.5.a describe), but nowhere in Article IX is a Monitor given the authority to compel an outcome, issue a binding order, or discharge a duty on another body's behalf. §9.5.b closes that gap by stating expressly what the rest of the Article implies structurally: a finding is not an action, and publishing a finding does not perform the duty the finding describes.

The design choice has a practical effect on how the whole monitoring apparatus operates. Under §9.5.a, a Monitor publishes audit findings and submits them to the constitutional institution responsible for the matter under review, and that institution must make its own compliance determination under applicable constitutional and statutory procedures. §9.5.b reinforces that sequence by making clear that the institution's duty to determine compliance, or to act within its operational authority, survives the Monitor's report untouched — the report is input, not substitute performance. The same logic connects to §9.1.b's definition of executive dereliction: the Executive Monitor can audit an executive officer for failing to perform a constitutionally mandated function, but the officer's obligation to perform that function was never created by the audit and is not satisfied by the audit's existence. The Monitor documents the failure; it does not step into the officer's shoes to cure it.

The failure mode this guards against is a predictable one in any system built around oversight reporting: a responsible body treating a critical or exculpatory Monitor finding as license to do nothing, on the theory that the finding itself has settled or discharged the matter. Without §9.5.b, a body could point to a published assessment — favorable or unfavorable — as a stand-in for exercising its own judgment and authority, effectively laundering inaction through the Monitor's paperwork. By stating that the obligation to perform duties and act within operational authority is independent of what any monitor report says, §9.5.b keeps responsibility located where the Constitution otherwise places it — with the body that holds the constitutional or statutory duty — rather than allowing it to migrate to, or be absorbed by, the oversight function that merely observes and publishes.

§9.7.text:
The Joint Monitor Council is built on the Institution Test: rather than creating a fourth oversight body, the Constitution turns the three existing Monitor Generals into a council whenever matters cross their separate jurisdictions. Each Monitor General individually holds a defined slice of oversight — the Legislative, Executive, and Judicial Monitors each watch a different set of institutions — and the Council exists only to coordinate where those slices meet and to oversee compliance with constitutional processes specifically assigned to it. This is a narrow, functional body, not a general supervisory layer above the three Monitors.

The internal mechanics are built for functioning despite partial absence while still requiring real agreement. Two of three Monitor Generals constitute quorum, so the Council can act without unanimous attendance, but decisions still require a majority of participating members, meaning a lone Monitor General present at quorum cannot carry a decision alone — at least two of the two or three present must agree. The requirement that dissenting positions be published to the NRS, the Republic's permanent, tamper-evident public record under the defining NRS provision, keeps disagreement visible rather than absorbed into a bare numerical outcome; a Monitor General who loses a vote still gets an on-record account of why, which guards against the appearance of false unanimity among three powerful, independent watchdogs. The Council's rule-making power is explicitly bounded: it may set compliance standards within its own constitutional mandate, but it may not exercise functions assigned to another constitutional institution and may not override an individual Monitor's independent authority. That second limit directly protects the structure established elsewhere for each Monitor General — their jurisdiction and independence belong to them individually, and the Council's coordinating role cannot be used to dilute or substitute for that individual authority, consistent with the principle that Monitor findings do not substitute for a responsible body's own obligations to act within its authority.

The audit duty is the Council's distinct, affirmative function: it must audit the National Record System itself at statutory intervals, checking operational compliance, accessibility, continuity, content integrity, and completeness of required publications. This closes a specific gap — the NRS is the backbone of transparency for the entire Constitution, including the Council's own dissent-publication duty, so someone independent of the system's day-to-day operation must verify that the record is actually working as designed. Assigning this to the three Monitor Generals collectively, rather than to any single Monitor or a new auditor, keeps the check inside the existing Monitor framework while ensuring no single Monitor General controls the audit of the record that documents everyone's conduct, including the Monitors' own suspensions and dissents.

§9.7.a.text:
§9.7.a creates an emergency suspension mechanism for a Monitor General, and it rests on a structural problem the Monitors themselves embody: each of the three Monitors is independent, and none has an ordinary superior who can discipline it. The Legislative Monitor audits the Legislature, the Executive Monitor audits the executive, the Judicial Monitor audits the judiciary — each watches a different branch, not each other. §9.7.a solves the "who watches the watchmen" problem by using the other two Monitors as the detection mechanism: where two of the three find evidence that the third has engaged in serious misconduct or abuse of office, they may recommend suspension by publishing their findings to the NRS. That publication requirement makes the triggering act itself a public record rather than a private or internal determination, consistent with the general practice of routing institutional findings through the NRS. The provision also forecloses a specific abuse path by stating that disagreement with a Monitor General's findings or conclusions is not grounds for suspension — two Monitors cannot use this protocol to neutralize a colleague merely because they dislike the colleague's audit conclusions; the trigger is misconduct or abuse of office, not substantive disagreement.

The design choice that keeps this mechanism from being self-dealing is that the two accusing Monitors never suspend the third themselves. Approval runs instead through an external institution matched to the audited Monitor's own domain: a Supreme Court majority approves suspension of the Legislative Monitor, the two legislative Speakers jointly approve suspension of the Executive Monitor, and both executives jointly approve suspension of the Judicial Monitor. Each approving body sits outside the chamber or office that Monitor audits, so the check on a Monitor's independence is lodged with an institution that has no direct stake in softening that Monitor's scrutiny of it. This mirrors the removal structure in §9.9(1), where initiation authority for misconduct removal likewise comes from "an institution outside the Monitor's audit mandate" — the two provisions use a parallel outside-the-audit-relationship logic even though they are separate mechanisms with separate triggers and consequences.

The 90-day ceiling on suspension, absent initiated removal proceedings, keeps suspension from becoming a standing disability imposed without ever testing the underlying misconduct claim through the removal process in §9.9. If removal proceedings are initiated, suspension may continue until their conclusion, but only subject to expedited independent judicial review of continuing necessity, and a court may terminate a suspension whose continuing necessity is not established — so the extended suspension is not open-ended either; it remains tethered to an ongoing judicial check. Suspension ends immediately if removal is rejected or concludes without removal, and the provision states plainly that suspension does not constitute removal and may not substitute for permanent removal — guarding against using a temporary emergency tool to accomplish a permanent ouster without ever meeting removal's own standards. During any suspension, acting authority operates under §9.1.d, so the audited office is not actually vacated; an Acting Monitor General drawn from the candidate pool exercises the Monitor's authority until the suspension ends or removal is resolved.

§9.8.text:
§9.8 sets up the general architecture that governs every constitutional candidate pool — the Judicial Pool defined in §9.4.a is one concrete instance of the structure this provision describes. The Elections Panel runs the pools, registries, and selection lotteries, while the Joint Monitor Council audits compliance with those requirements. This splits administration from oversight along lines already established elsewhere in Article IX: the Council's own provision describes it as a body that coordinates cross-Monitor matters and oversees compliance with constitutional processes assigned to it, so routing pool-compliance audit through the Council here is an application of the Institution Test rather than the creation of a new oversight body. Pool records being publicly accessible through the NRS gives this oversight a transparency backbone — anyone can check whether a pool is properly populated without waiting on a Monitor's own initiative.

The five-member floor in subsection (2) is a concrete structural safeguard against pool starvation — a pool that shrinks too far could let a single appointment or disqualification distort the field of eligible candidates, effectively giving whoever controls entry a chokehold on selection. The provision does not leave this to discretion: a deficiency must be published to the NRS, and the Elections Panel must act to restore the pool under statute. The public-disclosure requirement means a shrinking pool cannot be quietly managed; it forces the failure into the open NRS record where the Judicial Monitor's audit authority over the Elections Panel, noted in §9.1.c, and the Council's compliance oversight can both see it. Subsection (3)'s objective-criteria rule guards against a different abuse — using eligibility screening as a backdoor for ideological or political gatekeeping of pools that are supposed to supply judicial and other constitutional appointments. Excluding legal philosophy, judicial temperament, ideological orientation, and political association as grounds for exclusion keeps pool membership a pre-political, criteria-based determination rather than a policy lever, consistent with treating constitutional eligibility as something other than a matter of political preference. Subsection (4)'s guarantee of a published statement of reasons and timely judicial review for anyone excluded or removed gives that objective-criteria rule teeth — without a review channel, a biased exclusion decision could hide behind silence.

Subsection (5)'s prospective-only rule for eligibility changes protects settled expectations: someone already in a pool under the old criteria keeps their place even if the Legislature later tightens eligibility standards, which prevents retroactive purges dressed up as criteria updates. But that protection is explicitly bounded — it does not exempt a member from continuing constitutional eligibility requirements, specifically the prohibition on disqualifying financial interests under §7.10. That cross-reference matters because §7.10 defines a disqualifying interest as one creating a direct and material conflict with impartial exercise of official duties, and makes recusal self-executing; grandfathering a pool member against new eligibility rules could not be read to also shield them from that separate, ongoing conflict-of-interest check. The combination keeps §9.8 focused on the integrity of the pool's composition and gatekeeping process, while leaving financial-conflict enforcement entirely to its one home in §7.10 rather than duplicating it here.

§9.9.text:
§9.9 builds the removal of a Monitor General on a structural guard against self-protection: the institution that may initiate removal is always one standing outside that Monitor's audit mandate. The Legislative Monitor General, who under §9.1.a audits the Legislature, can be targeted only by either Consul — not by the body being audited. The Executive Monitor General can be targeted only by a legislative chamber, and the Judicial Monitor General, whose mandate under §9.1.c covers the courts and the Elections Panel, by either chamber or either Consul. This keeps the audited institution from controlling the removal of its own auditor. The initiating authority must publish its stated grounds to the NRS, so the basis for a removal attempt is a matter of public record before any vote occurs, and initiation alone does not suspend the Monitor General's authority — the office continues functioning unless suspended under some other constitutional mechanism. The Elections Panel must run a national referendum within 90 days of initiation or at the next regularly scheduled federal election, whichever comes first, and removal requires 60% of votes cast under the §7.3 supermajority standard, with no turnout requirement attached. If the referendum is not held within that window, the proceeding does not die — it continues, and the Monitor General keeps authority unless separately suspended.

A failed referendum carries its own consequence: no new proceeding may be brought against the same Monitor General on substantially the same grounds arising from the same conduct during that term, though materially new conduct or evidence reopens the door. This blocks repeated referenda from being used to wear down an officer who has already survived a vote on the same facts. Permanent incapacity runs on an entirely separate track from misconduct: it requires the other two Monitor Generals to determine incapacity and recommend removal to the Speaker, with removal itself needing two-thirds of each legislative chamber and both Consuls — a higher, non-electoral bar reflecting that incapacity is a factual rather than political judgment, reinforced by the explicit statement that disagreement with a Monitor's findings is not incapacity. Other constitutionally confirmed independent officers follow yet another path: initiation by one-third of either chamber, removal by two-thirds of the full seated membership of each chamber, on grounds the Legislature sets by statute, with changes to those categories applying only prospectively.

The provision depends on §7.3 for its vote threshold and on §9.1.a and §9.1.c to identify which institutions fall outside a given Monitor's mandate and are therefore eligible initiators. It also connects to §9.9.a, which names concealment of a disqualifying financial interest or failure to recuse as serious misconduct for removal purposes. Together these mechanics guard against an audited body capturing or intimidating its auditor, against incapacity being used as a political weapon against unfavorable findings, and against serial relitigation of the same removal grounds against a sitting Monitor General.

§9.9.a.text:
§9.9.a extends the ethics regime of §7.10 to the three Monitor Generals, but it cannot simply plug them into that provision's ordinary mechanism, because §7.10(2) routes disclosure to "the Monitor responsible for their office" — and a Monitor General has no superior Monitor to report to. The provision solves this by keeping the substantive requirements and schedule of §7.10 identical (what counts as a disqualifying financial interest, when disclosure happens, and the annual cycle) while changing the recipient: disclosure goes directly to the NRS rather than to another officeholder. This is why §7.10(2) itself carves Monitor Generals out of its ordinary reporting line — "Except for Monitor Generals as provided in Article IX" — and §9.9.a is the provision that fills that carve-out.

The clause "no Monitor reviews another Monitor General's disclosure" is the structural safeguard that makes direct NRS publication necessary rather than optional. Each Monitor General audits a different branch (Legislative, Executive, Judicial) and operates independently of the others; letting one Monitor General review a peer's financial disclosures would hand that Monitor General informational leverage over a co-equal officer with its own audit mandate, creating a channel for pressure or selective scrutiny between offices meant to check different branches rather than each other. Publishing straight to the NRS removes any single Monitor General as a gatekeeper over another's compliance record, so the disclosure becomes a matter of public record rather than a peer-reviewed filing. This also preserves the one-place-only design of financial disclosure: the same substantive rule in §7.10 governs everyone, but the reporting channel is adapted rather than duplicated for this one category of officer.

The second sentence supplies the consequence that makes the disclosure duty meaningful: concealment of a disqualifying financial interest, or failure to recuse where required, is designated "serious misconduct for purposes of §9.9" — the removal provision. This ties §9.9.a directly into the removal machinery of §9.9(1)-(3): for a Monitor General, removal on this ground must be initiated by an institution outside that Monitor's own audit mandate (the relevant Consul(s) or legislative chamber(s)), subjected to a national referendum requiring 60% approval, with a failed referendum barring a repeat proceeding on the same grounds absent materially new conduct or evidence. Without this misconduct designation, a concealed conflict or unrecused decision by a Monitor General would have no defined constitutional consequence, since no peer Monitor reviews the disclosure to catch it internally and refer it onward. By making concealment or non-recusal a removal-triggering offense and relying on public NRS disclosure as the means of exposure, the provision guards against the specific failure mode of a Monitor General hiding a financial conflict precisely because no other Monitor is positioned, or authorized, to check that disclosure for them.

§10.1.text:
Section 10.1 establishes the National Record System as the Republic's permanent, tamper-evident, freely accessible public record, and its core design choice is to make publication automatic rather than provision-by-provision: every constitutional act, order, finding, certification, designation, declaration, and determination is published to the NRS without any separate textual instruction to do so. This embodies the Transparency Test's demand that every exercise of constitutional authority leave a public record — instead of scattering publication duties across dozens of provisions, the obligation lives in one place and attaches automatically to the category of acts described. Official records are declared property of the Republic, and officers are barred from removing them from Republic custody, keeping them as personal property, or destroying them except as applicable law authorizes, which prevents an officer from privatizing or erasing the record of their own official conduct.

Electoral records receive an explicit, categorical rule: voter registration, ballot counts, audit trails, certification documents, campaign-finance records, electoral-administration records, direct-democracy records, and constitutional-amendment records must be published within the applicable timeframe, and no classification exception applies to them at all — a stronger rule than the general classification regime in §10.2, which permits withholding for national-security grounds subject to a 25-year ceiling. This categorical exclusion guards against the specific failure mode of election results or audit trails being shielded from public view under a national-security pretext. The carve-outs for ballot secrecy under §11.2 and personal information under §1.7 keep this transparency duty from colliding with the NVS's guarantee that no vote can be linked to a voter. Where the Constitution sets no specific publication timeline, subsection (4) defaults to "as soon as possible," and subsection (5) locks in tamper-evidence by forbidding deletion, alteration, or reclassification after publication — corrections become new entries alongside the original rather than replacing it, preserving a complete history rather than a edited one.

Subsection (6) is the system's only access-restriction valve, and it is deliberately narrow: the NRS Panel must vote unanimously that a record poses an imminent, specific, documented threat to individual safety, and the resulting restriction lasts only 30 days unless a statutorily designated court confirms it on the narrowest possible grounds and sets its own duration; an unconfirmed restriction cannot be reimposed on the same or substantially similar grounds, closing off repeated relitigation of the same suppression attempt. This is a temporary-confidentiality mechanism with a hard default toward restoration, consistent with disallowing permanent withholding. Subsection (7) guards against capture or failure of the NRS itself: the JM runs a physically independent parallel authentication system that preserves constitutional acts with full effect, migrates records with original timestamps once the NRS is restored, and becomes the constitutional record outright if the NRS stays down for 180 days — a defined failure state ensuring the Republic's record never depends on a single system staying operational. The Legislature sets technical standards for both systems by statute, and this provision's inclusion among the oversight provisions requiring Popular Ratification to amend reflects that the record-keeping architecture checking the branches is itself insulated from easy alteration by those branches.

§10.2.text:
§10.2 sets the substantive and temporal limits on government secrecy, and it does so by pinning classification to a single justification: protection of national security. That ground cannot be invented case-by-case — it must trace to a statute or to an executive standard the classifying executive has published to the NRS before the record is ever classified, and a statute overrides any conflicting executive standard. This creates a rule-of-law anchor for classification: the standard has to exist publicly, in advance, so that classification cannot be justified retroactively by a rationale invented after the fact. The classifying authority then must state the specific ground relied on at the time of classification, tying each act of secrecy to a traceable, named justification rather than a generic invocation of security. This satisfies the Actor Test by naming the classifying executive as the holder of the power and requiring a contemporaneous, recorded reason for its exercise.

The 25-year ceiling, and the mechanism for extending it, show the provision's graceful-degradation design: secrecy is temporary by default, and permanence requires an affirmative, bounded act. A single five-year extension becomes available only when the classifying executive publishes a justification to the EM, which assesses the justification against the applicable statutory standard and publishes its finding to the NRS. Because EM findings are not binding on any constitutional actor and are not a prerequisite for any legal proceeding or governmental function, an adverse EM finding does not block the extension — the extension proceeds regardless of what the EM concludes. The extension therefore stays within the classifying executive's own discretion; conditioning it on a favorable EM finding would have made Monitor findings binding, which would break the information-only architecture the Monitor offices rest on throughout the Constitution. What the EM step guarantees is not a veto but sunlight: whatever the executive decides, the justification and the EM's assessment of it both become public record, so the public can see exactly what reasoning extended the secrecy, even though that record cannot force a different outcome.

Once classification lapses — at 25 years, or at 30 if the single extension was taken — declassification is automatic. The NRS Panel publishes the declassified record within 30 days after expiration, and the text is explicit that this obligation requires no further government act, so no official discretion or additional step can delay release past that window. This closes off the failure mode the whole provision is built to prevent: a classification regime that becomes permanent in practice through bureaucratic inertia or silent non-action, since §10.1 separately makes the NRS the self-executing public record of constitutional acts with records that cannot be deleted or altered after publication. The provision also gives any person with standing a continuing petition right to the statutorily designated court for release before expiration, and the court must order release of any portion not actually required by a ground consistent with statute and the Constitution, publishing redactions and their grounds alongside whatever is released — pairing the automatic time-based release with an available judicial check against classification exceeding its own stated justification.

§11.1.text:
§11.1 establishes two of the Republic's independent agencies — the NRS Panel and the Elections Panel — and builds structural protections around them that reflect the core principle that whoever controls the record of votes and the machinery of elections cannot be the same actor whose power depends on the outcome. Subsection (3) makes both panels independent agencies under §3.9.a, meaning each is operationally independent not just of the executives and Legislature but of each other in exercising its respective functions — the panel that certifies results is walled off from the panel that maintains the permanent record, and neither answers operationally to the other. The Elections Panel's enumerated functions in (2) — maintaining the National Voting System, setting technical and administrative standards, certifying equipment, auditing State compliance, administering referendums and lotteries, and certifying federal election results — sit entirely within that independent domain, drawing on the general rule in §3.9 that the Legislature may organize but may not impair the independence of a function this Constitution assigns to an independent agency.

The appointment structure in (4) is the provision's central anti-capture mechanism: each panel must hold no fewer than five seated members at all times, and no single appointing authority may hold a majority of appointments to either panel within any single electoral term. This rule exists because the body that certifies federal election results must not be assembled by the very officials whose elections it certifies. That logic carries directly into subsection (6)'s vacancy-filling design. When a panel falls below the five-member floor, the remaining members — not an external executive — designate Acting members by majority vote from among the panel's own qualified civil servants, for a period set by statute capped at 180 days; the Civic Consul designates only where the remaining members are unable to, and even then Civic Consul-designated Acting members can never constitute a majority of the panel's seated membership. This structure replaced an earlier version that let the Civic Consul unilaterally appoint Acting members whenever a panel fell below the floor, with no limit on how many could be made at once — a design that would have let multiple simultaneous vacancies hand one executive a working majority on the very body certifying that executive's own election results. The current text closes that gap by keeping designation authority inside the panel itself and capping the Consul's fallback role.

Subsection (5) governs a narrower problem: emergency technical response. Each panel may adopt temporary measures against imminent security threats or system failures by majority vote, but those measures cannot touch electoral rules, timelines, or NRS record permanence, and they expire after 72 hours; a fresh measure requires a new published determination of imminent threat rather than an automatic renewal. This prevents an emergency justification from becoming a standing tool to alter substantive electoral or record-keeping rules under the guise of security response. Read together, the five-member floor, the appointment-majority bar, the panel-first designation sequence, and the 72-hour emergency ceiling all guard against the same failure mode from different angles: a single executive or appointing authority quietly accumulating control over the institutions that record and certify the Republic's elections.

§11.2.text:
§11.2 fixes the technical and legal properties that the National Voting System must satisfy, and it does so by treating secrecy, auditability, and resilience as a single bundle rather than separate goods to be traded against one another. The text requires all three "simultaneously": it must be technically impossible to link a vote to a voter even during a post-election audit, aggregate results must be mathematically verifiable by anyone with NRS access, each voter must be able to verify their own vote in a way that cannot be turned into proof for a third party, and the system must keep functioning in degraded conditions without sacrificing either secrecy or auditability. This is a pre-political design floor on how elections are run, not a policy choice about who wins them — it constrains the machinery itself. The individual-verifiability clause is worth isolating: it gives the voter a private check on correctness while explicitly closing the door on using that same check to sell or coerce a vote, which is what keeps a verifiable system from collapsing into a coercible one.

The provision also locks down what can be done with the data the NVS generates. Information from the system, including participation records, may be used or shared only to administer, audit, or certify the relevant election or petition, or for judicial review of its results — a closed list of purposes, not an open-ended administrative convenience. Eligibility verification is barred from storing or exposing voter identity within the NVS itself, which is what makes the secrecy guarantee structurally enforceable rather than merely promised: if identity never enters the system, it cannot later be extracted from it, by audit or otherwise. The provision adds a non-discrimination rule against the States: no State may impose requirements or intermediaries that effectively reduce NVS access or impose burdens beyond those of direct NVS participation, preventing a State from reintroducing friction or exposure through its own administrative layer that the NVS itself is built to avoid. Finally, the Elections Panel is given an affirmative duty to inform every eligible citizen of their federal races and how to vote before each federal election, naming the Elections Panel as the actor who must act and the eligible citizenry as the beneficiary of that information duty.

§11.2 depends on §11.1 for its institutional footing: §11.1 is what establishes the Elections Panel as the body that builds and maintains the NVS and sets federal election standards, so the properties and restrictions in §11.2 bind an entity already given operational control rather than inventing new machinery. §11.3 in turn treats "the requirements of §11.2" as an enforceable standard — a State audit finding a material failure to meet them triggers publication, notice, a statutory cure period, and, if uncured, direct Elections Panel administration of that election — but §11.3 supplies its own separate trigger and remedy rather than altering what §11.2 itself requires. The failure mode §11.2 is built against is a voting system that can be deanonymized after the fact, gamed through unverifiable tallies, knocked offline without a safe fallback, mined for participation data beyond election administration, used to coerce voters through provable ballots, or quietly throttled by State-level barriers that defeat the guarantee in substance while leaving the NVS itself technically intact.

§11.3.text:
§11.3 enforces federal election standards against a State that fails to meet them, backing the Elections Panel's audit authority under §11.1(2) with a real consequence. §11.1 gives the Panel the job of setting administrative and technical standards for federal elections and auditing State compliance with those standards, and of enforcing the NVS properties — ballot secrecy, public auditability, and resilience — defined in §11.2. Auditing without a consequence would leave the Panel able only to describe a problem, not fix it. §11.3 closes that gap: once the Panel finds through audit that a State's election administration materially fails to meet §11.1 standards or §11.2 requirements, it must publish the finding to the NRS and notify the State formally, converting an internal audit judgment into a public record and a direct notice to the party responsible for correcting it.

The operative sequence in §11.3 runs on a defined cure period, a conditional pre-election remedy, and an automatic-reversion takeover. The State gets the period set by statute to cure the identified failures — the text does not fix a number of days itself, leaving that interval to statute. If the finding comes before an election, the Panel may withhold certification of results for the affected districts, but only pending compliance or a special election called under §7.2.a; this is a holding action tied to the cure process, not a penalty on voters. If the State does not cure within the cure period, the consequence is direct: the Elections Panel takes over administration of the relevant federal election within that State, but strictly for that electoral period only, and State administration resumes automatically once the period ends — no further act or petition is needed to restore State control. This scopes the remedy tightly to the specific election at issue rather than creating an open-ended federal takeover of State election machinery, and it returns authority to the State without requiring the State to re-earn it through a separate restoration step.

The final sentence — that neither a finding of non-compliance nor withholding of certification affects the validity of votes cast — protects the votes themselves from the consequences of institutional failure. This tracks the ballot-secrecy and public-auditability guarantees in §11.2: a State's administrative failure is a problem between the State and the Panel, not a defect attributable to the individual voter's act of voting. Structurally, §11.3 depends on §11.1 and §11.2 for its substantive triggers — it has no independent standard of its own, only the audit finding against those external benchmarks — and it borrows the special-election mechanism from §7.2.a rather than creating a new one. The provision guards against a State using administrative noncompliance, deliberate or not, to degrade federal election standards, secrecy, or auditability with impunity, while preventing that same risk from being visited on voters whose ballots were cast in good faith under a noncompliant system. The automatic reversion also guards against the opposite failure mode — a federal takeover of State election administration becoming indefinite rather than confined to the single affected electoral period.

§12.1.text:
§12.1 establishes the Republic as a social state, which operates as a pre-political constitutional commitment rather than an ordinary policy choice: the text itself entitles every Inhabitant — defined as every person present within the Republic's jurisdiction, not merely citizens — to conditions of life consistent with human dignity, and fixes that entitlement through three mandatory guarantees named in the text itself: universally accessible basic healthcare, social assistance sufficient to assist in maintaining basic material conditions, and free compulsory education for every child. By writing the entitlement and its three guarantees directly into the constitutional text, rather than leaving them to ordinary statute, the provision takes the existence of these guarantees out of the Legislature's discretion even though the Legislature retains substantial power over their content.

The design choice that does the structural work is the division between what the Legislature controls and what it cannot touch. The Legislature establishes the framework and adequacy standards for the three guarantees by statute — meaning the specifics of eligibility, benefit levels, healthcare delivery mechanisms, and educational standards are left to ordinary legislative judgment, which can be updated over time. But the text draws a hard line: no statutory adjustment may eliminate or substantially impair the constitutional guarantees established by this section. This creates a floor beneath which statutory policymaking cannot go, regardless of fiscal pressure, political majority, or shifting policy preference. The parent-or-guardian direction clause operates within this same framework — parents or guardians may direct their children's education, but only within public standards, meaning the Legislature's framework-setting power over education extends to bounding that choice without displacing the underlying free compulsory education guarantee itself. Naming guardians alongside parents covers a child with no available parent, such as a ward of the State or one under court-appointed guardianship, and matches the phrase "parent or guardian" in §5.3; where the State is itself the guardian the protection is thinner, since the State also sets the framework.

Compliance monitoring is assigned to the Executive Monitor, which assesses the three guarantees annually. The Executive Monitor is the body that audits executive officers, ministers, agencies, and the Monetary Authority for constitutional compliance and for dereliction of constitutional duties — failure to perform a constitutionally mandated function within the required period, absent circumstances genuinely beyond the officer's control. Housing compliance assessment in the Executive Monitor rather than creating a new oversight body reflects reliance on an existing constitutional institution for this function, and the annual assessment gives the floor-against-impairment language a recurring checkpoint rather than leaving it to surface only through litigation or political dispute. The provision's core failure mode is legislative erosion of a constitutional guarantee through ordinary statutory amendment — a majority deciding, guarantee by guarantee, to hollow out healthcare access, social assistance, or compulsory education under the appearance of routine adjustment. The anti-impairment clause blocks that path by making elimination or substantial impairment constitutionally off-limits regardless of the vote margin behind it, while still leaving the Legislature free to set, and revise, the adequacy standards and administrative framework through which the guarantees are actually delivered.

§12.1.a.text:
The Monetary Authority sits inside Article XII's social-state framework but is built as an independent agency under the general rule of §3.9, not as a freestanding body — the provision expressly invokes §3.9.a for its operational independence and §3.9 for its governing framework "except as this section provides." That reliance is the Institution Test at work: rather than drafting a new independence regime, §12.1.a borrows the Republic's existing apparatus for independent statutory agencies and layers monetary-specific rules on top where the generic rule would be insufficient. §3.9 already establishes that an independent agency's leadership serves fixed terms and may be removed only for conduct, incapacity, or incompetence, never policy disagreement, and that qualification rules may not be designed to screen out people for their political or policy views. §12.1.a's own sentence that "disagreement over monetary policy, economic judgment, or a lawful certification is not cause for removal" restates that §3.9 removal standard in terms specific to monetary functions — currency issuance, fiscal integrity certification, and National Endowment duties — making explicit that a certification the Executive or Legislature dislikes is not grounds to oust the people who issued it.

Where the provision departs from the generic §3.9 template, it does so because monetary power carries distinct risks. Ordinary independent-agency appointments are left to statute under §3.9 ("unless this Constitution provides otherwise, statute governs... appointments"), but here the Constitution itself provides otherwise: principal decision-makers must come through an independent candidate process and win confirmation by two-thirds of the Senate, a threshold matching the supermajority used elsewhere for high-stakes confirmations. No single officer or institution may appoint a majority of decision-makers, and terms must be staggered so that ordinary electoral turnover cannot replace the entire leadership at once. Together these three mechanics — independent nomination, supermajority confirmation, and staggered terms — guard against the same failure mode from three angles: a single election cycle or a single appointing authority capturing the currency-issuing power and bending monetary policy to short-term political ends. The exclusive-issuance clause closes a parallel gap, making certain no competing body can create parallel legal tender and sidestep the Authority's control entirely.

The vacancy clause — that a vacancy does not suspend or transfer the Monetary Authority's constitutional functions — defines the provision's failure state consistent with the Graceful Degradation Test: currency issuance and fiscal certification cannot simply stop because a seat is empty, and no other body inherits those functions by default. This connects to the sibling reporting duty in §12.1.b, which keeps the Authority's independence checked by publication rather than by removal, and to the social-state guarantees in §12.1, which depend on sustained fiscal integrity to be funded at all. The provision was split out from the broader Social State section specifically to give the Authority its own confirmation, appointment, and removal rules distinct from the general independent-agency template, reflecting that monetary power needs insulation calibrated more tightly than ordinary agency independence provides.

§12.1.b.text:
§12.1.b establishes a recurring, mandatory disclosure obligation for the Monetary Authority: a State of the Economy report, published to the NRS, the Assembly, the Legat Consul, and the Civic Consul no less than semi-annually, with statute permitted to require greater frequency but not less. The report must independently assess economic conditions, fiscal sustainability, and performance against the Republic's fiscal obligations, identify areas requiring improvement, and describe the MA's own actions within its authority. This is a transparency mechanism applied to an independent agency wielding exclusive currency-issuance and monetary-policy power under §12.1.a — power that, by its nature, operates through technical judgments not easily visible to elected officials or the public. Requiring publication to the NRS, the record-keeping system named elsewhere in the constitution, ties the report to the durable public-record function, while simultaneous distribution to the Assembly, Legat Consul, and Civic Consul ensures every branch with a stake in fiscal and economic conditions receives the same information at the same time, rather than the MA briefing one office and leaving others to learn secondhand.

The design choice of a floor rather than a ceiling — "no less than semi-annually, or more frequently as statute requires" — fixes a constitutional minimum that ordinary legislation cannot weaken, while leaving the Assembly free to legislate more frequent reporting if circumstances warrant. This matters because §12.1.a makes the MA's principal decision-makers removable only through structured process, not through disagreement over monetary policy, economic judgment, or lawful certification; the reporting duty is the compensating mechanism that keeps an insulated, hard-to-remove body answerable through information even though it cannot be answerable through ordinary removal. The report's required content — independent assessment of conditions and fiscal sustainability, performance against fiscal obligations, needed improvements, and the MA's own actions — gives the recipient bodies a substantive basis for evaluating the MA's stewardship without granting them a formal override of its monetary authority.

The provision depends directly on §12.1.a for what the MA is and what it does: the reporting duty only makes sense against that section's grant of exclusive currency-issuance and monetary-policy authority and its insulation of principal decision-makers from removal over policy disagreement. It also depends on the Civic Consul's domain under §2.5, which includes social-state administration under Article XII, and on the Assembly as defined in §3.2, both named recipients whose oversight and legislative roles make the report relevant to their functions. The failure mode this guards against is an independent, currency-issuing authority operating in an information vacuum — making monetary and fiscal judgments that affect the Republic's fiscal obligations and economic conditions while elected and appointed officials have no regular, guaranteed channel for finding out what it has done or why. By fixing a recurring floor for disclosure to every body with a legitimate interest, the provision prevents the MA's structural independence from becoming structural opacity.

§12.2.text:
§12.2 embodies the constitutional principle that the power of the purse belongs to the legislature acting on executive-prepared proposals, while fiscal continuity cannot depend on that legislature actually reaching agreement. The provision splits into two logics: an origination and transparency regime for the ordinary budget, and an automatic fallback for when the ordinary process fails. Under subsection (1), each Consul — not the Assembly — drafts the budget for their own domain and submits it to the Assembly, with publication to the NRS required at the moment of submission, not after enactment. The deadline is set by statute, with a 120-day-before-fiscal-year default if no statute exists, and critically, a Consul's failure to submit does not delay or bar the process — the Assembly's budget work proceeds regardless. This closes an obvious bad-faith avenue: an executive officer cannot freeze the budget cycle by simply withholding a submission.

Subsection (2) ties fiscal practice to a sustainability obligation — keeping public finances, including public debt, sustainable while the Republic fulfills its constitutional obligations, a test that looks forward without a stated horizon — and assigns the Monetary Authority an assessment role — mandatory after enactment, optional at either chamber's request beforehand — which keeps fiscal information flowing to the legislature without giving the MA any power to block or amend what the Assembly enacts. The more consequential mechanism is subsection (3): if no budget is enacted by the start of the fiscal year (or an earlier statutory deadline), or if an enacted budget is repealed through the optional referendum process under §13.1, an interim automatic appropriation takes effect "by constitutional operation" — meaning it requires no further legislative or executive act to trigger. That appropriation is confined to four categories: judicial operations, active defense authorizations under §14.2, and social state continuity under §12.1; civil service compensation; resources sufficient to maintain duties of institutions under §3.10; and debt service. Subsection (4) fixes the appropriation at the prior year's inflation-adjusted level and bars new or expanded programs under it, so the fallback sustains existing government function without letting anyone use a budget impasse to either starve the state or smuggle in new spending by default. This is a narrower, structurally distinct instrument from the Legat Consul's extraordinary defensive expenditure authority in §12.2.a, which is a discretionary emergency power tied to active or imminent attack and continues only while that condition persists — the §12.2(3) interim appropriation instead activates automatically from the calendar or from a referendum repeal, with no discretionary trigger and no stated expiration beyond enactment of a budget.

The referendum linkage matters because §13.1 confirms that citizens may repeal legislation including appropriations, but a referendum may not amend an appropriation or substitute a different amount — so repeal of a budget law can only return the Republic to the §12.2(3) fallback, never rewrite the budget itself. Subsection (6)'s requirement that the Legislature fund the National Endowment in years of fiscal surplus, with the Executive Monitor assessing compliance annually, is a distinct, narrower fiscal-discipline rule riding alongside the general budget process, giving the EM an oversight function without enforcement power beyond assessment. Together these mechanisms guard against two failure modes: an executive stalling the budget by nonsubmission, and a legislative or referendum deadlock collapsing government function — both addressed by making continuity automatic, transparent, and strictly bounded rather than discretionary.

§12.2.a.text:
§12.2.a carves out a narrow exception to the principle, stated in §12.2, that the annual budget originates in the Assembly and that spending runs through the appropriation process. The exception exists because a sudden or imminent attack can require money to be spent faster than the Assembly's ordinary process can move, and the provision addresses that timing gap rather than displacing the Assembly's general control over fiscal affairs. The Legat Consul, who under §2.1 holds authority over military command and force employment, is the actor given power to authorize expenditure in this narrow circumstance — a sensible fit, since this is the officer already responsible for operational defense decisions within that domain.

The design choice is tightly bounded on every axis stated in the text. The trigger is conjunctive: there must be an active or imminent attack, the needed expenditure must exceed available appropriations, and the Assembly must be unable to act — all three conditions are required, not just one. The authorized scope is limited to expenditure "necessary for the immediate defense of the Republic," not general military or foreign-affairs spending. Two consequences attach to the Legat Consul's exercise of this power: a reporting duty to the Speaker of the Assembly "without undue delay," which connects this mechanism to the Assembly defined in §3.2 as the body that selects its own Speaker and controls its own procedures, and a sunset rule — the authority "continues only while the conditions requiring its exercise persist." Once the Assembly is able to act again, it "must exercise its appropriation authority as soon as it is able," meaning the ordinary budget process defined in §12.2 resumes control over the spending rather than the extraordinary authorization becoming a permanent substitute for it.

This provision guards against two opposite failure modes. Without it, an attack that outpaces the Assembly's ability to convene or appropriate could leave the Republic unable to fund immediate defense, since §12.2 otherwise channels all spending through Assembly-originated appropriations. With it, but without the conditions and reporting duty, a Legat Consul could claim open-ended spending authority detached from any actual emergency, or could continue spending under this authority after the Assembly regained the ability to act. The conjunctive trigger prevents the power from being invoked merely because spending is convenient or appropriations are tight; the "unable to act" condition confines it to genuine Assembly incapacity rather than mere delay or disagreement; the reporting duty to the Speaker creates a point of accountability back to the legislative body even while it cannot yet act formally; and the persistence-based sunset, paired with the Assembly's own duty to resume its appropriation authority "as soon as it is able," prevents the extraordinary expenditure power from outliving the emergency that justified it or from becoming a standing parallel budget process alongside the one the Assembly ordinarily controls.

§12.3.text:
§12.3 establishes the Legislature's exclusive power to levy taxes, duties, and tariffs by statute, and pairs that power with a single consolidated fund through which nearly all public money must flow. This is a classic power-of-the-purse arrangement: taxation and spending authority are held by the elected legislative body, not scattered across executive actors, which ties revenue extraction to democratic accountability rather than administrative discretion. States, Territories, and local governments keep their own taxing authority within their jurisdictions, but that authority is expressly made subject to §12.5's internal commerce rule, which bars a State or Territory from imposing more burdensome requirements on goods or activity from another State or Territory than on its own. The provision's history shows this section was restored to the document along with two others, placed back into Article XII as the Legislature's exclusive-taxing and National Revenue Fund provision; a later audit removed "Associated Communities" from the rate-setting language because Associated Communities are sovereign equals under §20.2, and the Republic unilaterally setting their tax rates would have contradicted that equal-sovereignty principle — the Legislature's exclusive authority is accordingly bounded to the Republic itself, States, and Territories.

The Fund mechanism is the provision's structural core: all public money received by the Republic, other than the National Endowment's assets, must be deposited into the National Revenue Fund, and no money may leave that Fund except by appropriation. The National Endowment's exclusion matters because that reserve fund, as defined in §12.4, operates independently of the annual budget process under the Monetary Authority's management, so folding its assets into the general Fund would subject a dedicated backstop reserve to ordinary appropriation competition. The appropriation requirement for withdrawals explicitly includes the interim appropriation under §12.2 — meaning that when no annual budget is enacted by the start of the fiscal year, the automatic interim appropriation that takes effect by constitutional operation is itself treated as a valid appropriation for Fund-withdrawal purposes, so the "no withdrawal without appropriation" rule is not suspended during a budget gap but satisfied through that mechanism.
