Operating consistently with Article I means the mechanism cannot be used to evade whatever foundational rights or structural limits Article I supplies, even though it is pursuing accountability for a predecessor government's violations. The termination rule gives the mechanism a built-in failure state — it does not need a separate repeal vote to end; it simply expires when its statutory mandate runs out, which prevents a transitional body from calcifying into a permanent institution through sheer inertia. This provision sits near other transition-era mechanisms in Article XIX, such as the temporary review mechanism for predecessor classified material and the general rule on lawful temporary institutions, but each of those operates under its own trigger and duration; §19.8's gate, duration, and expansion rule belong only to it and are not carried over from those neighboring provisions. Together, the supermajority gate, the statute's mandatory specificity, the matching-threshold expansion rule, and the automatic sunset work as layered checks against the single underlying risk the provision is built around: a transitional accountability body that outlives its purpose or outgrows its original mandate without the same broad consent that created it.

§19.9.text:
§19.9 sets the general rule that governs every place in this Constitution where a permanent institution is required but not yet operating. Subsection (1) puts the duty on "the responsible authorities" to establish any constitutionally required permanent institution "in accordance with law" — naming an actor and an obligation rather than leaving the gap to inertia. Subsection (2) then bounds what fills that gap: a lawful temporary institution may exercise only the functions necessary to preserve constitutional continuity or rights, and only until the corresponding permanent institution becomes constitutionally capable of exercising those functions. This is a scope ceiling, not a grant of ordinary governing power — a temporary body cannot expand its own mandate beyond continuity and rights-preservation, and its authority ends automatically once the permanent institution is capable, without need for a separate termination act. The provision also supplies its own enforcement path: failure to establish a required institution is subject to judicial review, and a court of competent jurisdiction may compel the responsible authorities to act and may authorize temporary measures to preserve continuity or rights in the meantime. That gives the obligation in (1) a concrete consequence — a court, not a political body, can force compliance — closing off the possibility that a required institution simply never gets built because no one with power to delay it wants it built.

Subsection (3) addresses a specific instance of this same structural problem: the move from predecessor voting infrastructure to the National Voting System. It assigns the transition duty to the Legislature, which §3.1 defines as the Assembly and Senate acting together through the ordinary legislative process, and requires that the transition be established "by statute" and happen "without interrupting democratic participation." Unlike the general rule in (1)-(2), this clause names a specific actor (the Legislature) and a specific vehicle (statute) for one named transitional function, rather than leaving the method to whichever "responsible authorities" happen to hold the relevant power elsewhere in the transition framework. It sits alongside the caretaker-capacity rule for predecessor officials and institutions and the capability-triggered handover rule for Republic institutions assuming authority individually as each becomes capable — both of which describe the same continuity logic in other domains, with the permanent institution's constitutional capability, not an external date, operating as the trigger for transfer.

The failure mode this guards against is a gap in constitutional government: a required body that never gets established, or a "temporary" body that outlives its necessity or expands past continuity-and-rights preservation into ordinary governance it was never given a mandate to exercise. By pairing the establishment duty with a judicially enforceable remedy, and by capping temporary authority at what continuity or rights require, the provision prevents both failure modes — permanent vacancy and permanent improvisation — from becoming settled arrangements. The voting-transition clause applies the identical logic to a single high-stakes case: without a statutory bridge naming the Legislature as responsible actor, a changeover in voting infrastructure could otherwise stall or interrupt the exercise of democratic participation during the handover itself.

§19.10.text:
§19.10 solves a one-time problem: a brand-new Senate and a brand-new Supreme Court cannot start with every seat up for election or reappointment at the same moment, because that would recreate the instability the staggered-term structures in §3.5 and §4.3 are designed to prevent. The provision answers this by assigning the first cohort of senators and the first class of justices to varied initial terms, chosen by public lot, so that from the very first seating the bodies already have the staggered turnover that steady-state law expects. For the Senate, subsection (1) splits the first-seated senators into three roughly equal cohorts serving two, four, and six years respectively, with six-year terms applying to everyone thereafter — matching the six-year staggered term structure already fixed in §3.5(1). For the Supreme Court, subsection (2) splits the founding justices into three classes serving four, eight, and twelve years, after which §4.3 and §4.4 govern ordinary term length, selection, and vacancy-filling. The lot in both cases is conducted by the Elections Panel, and for the Senate it must be published to the NRS before the new senators take the constitutional oath — a public record requirement that lets anyone verify the cohort assignment was random and not manipulated to favor particular incumbents.

The lottery mechanism is the design choice doing the real work here: rather than letting the founding legislature or an appointing authority hand-pick who gets the short, medium, or long term, the text takes the decision out of anyone's discretion by binding it to public lot administered by an existing body, the Elections Panel, rather than inventing a new one. This reflects the general pattern of using existing institutions for a function that doesn't need a bespoke actor. The Senate lot's requirement that it be completed and published before senators take their oath ties the randomization to a fixed, verifiable moment, closing any window in which assignments could be adjusted after the fact once the actual composition of the incoming class is known.

§19.10 depends closely on the ordinary-term provisions it is staggering into existence. The Senate side relies on §3.5's six-year, two-per-State structure and its own internal succession rules, which is why §19.10(1) only sets the unequal founding terms and then hands off entirely to the six-year cycle already fixed there. The judicial side is explicit that "founding service under this subsection constitutes the justice's single term" for purposes of §4.3 and §4.4 — meaning a founding justice assigned a four-, eight-, or twelve-year initial term does not get an additional ordinary term afterward under §4.3's single non-renewable term rule; the founding assignment exhausts that justice's entire tenure. This guards against a founding-era loophole in which a justice could use an unusually long or short founding term as a stepping stone to a second, further term, defeating the non-renewability §4.3 establishes for ordinary appointments. By using lot rather than appointment, and by publishing the Senate's lot result before the oath, §19.10 forecloses the failure mode of insiders engineering who gets the longer or shorter founding term to entrench allies or disadvantage rivals at the republic's most vulnerable, least-tested moment.

§20.1.text:
§20.1 establishes the foundational premise for the entire Associated Communities framework: an Associated Community is not a part of the Republic but a sovereign political community outside it, linked only by a consensual compact. This is a pre-political structural fact rather than a policy choice — the provision does not grant sovereignty to these communities as a privilege the Republic extends, it recognizes sovereignty that exists independently and defines the relationship as one between two sovereign parties. That framing matters because everything else in Article XX — equal-party compact terms in §20.2, the bar on compelled government form, and the termination rights in §20.4 — only makes sense if the baseline is two sovereigns dealing with each other at arm's length rather than a central government administering a subordinate unit.

The design choice here is to make two distinct populations eligible for this status through a single doorway: recognized Indigenous nations under Article XVI, and any independent nation outside the Republic. The provision does not create a new procedure for Indigenous nations' sovereignty — it relies on Article XVI's existing recognition framework as the gateway, which is the provision defining what counts as a recognized Indigenous nation for this purpose. That cross-reference was corrected over the document's revision history: an earlier version pointed to a different article before being fixed to properly cite Article XVI, the actual home of Indigenous recognition, rather than an unrelated article. By routing eligibility through Article XVI instead of re-litigating recognition criteria inside Article XX, §20.1 avoids duplicating protections that already live elsewhere — consistent with keeping each protection in exactly one place. For independent nations, no comparable external gateway is specified; the text simply opens status to "any independent nation outside the Republic," placing the two eligible categories on the same footing as potential compact partners without a specified subordinate test.

Because §20.1 defines the relationship as outside-the-Republic and consensual, it structurally forecloses certain failure modes that the rest of the Article then makes explicit: §20.2 bars the Republic from dictating the Associated Community's form of government, and §20.4 bars either party from preventing, penalizing, or compelling continued association against an unwilling sovereign's own governance decision. Those downstream guarantees are coherent only because §20.1 has already fixed the character of the relationship as compact-based rather than hierarchical. If this provision were removed or reworded to describe Associated Communities as internal subdivisions rather than external sovereigns, the equal-party language in §20.2 and the termination protections in §20.4 would lose their anchor, since there would no longer be a clear baseline establishing that the Republic and the Associated Community meet as two sovereigns rather than as government and subject. The provision's core function is thus definitional: it names the actors (the Republic and the Associated Community) as sovereign equals under a compact, and that naming is what prevents the relationship from being quietly reinterpreted as one of authority and subordination elsewhere in the Article.

§20.2.text:
§20.2 establishes the baseline legal character of the relationship created by Article XX: the Republic and an Associated Community meet as equal sovereign parties to a compact, not as a central government and a subordinate unit. This tracks the Democratic Legitimacy Test's distinction between pre-political structural limits and ordinary policy choices — equal sovereignty is not a benefit the Republic extends at its discretion but a structural description of what kind of relationship this is, fixed before any particular compact's terms are negotiated. The provision does two things with that premise: it authorizes the compact to establish representation, consultation, and participation arrangements between the parties, and it forecloses one specific condition the Republic might otherwise try to impose — a required form of government for the Associated Community. The equal-sovereignty characterization is not merely descriptive; it has been treated elsewhere as a binding constraint on the Republic's own power, since a later audit removed Associated Communities from the Legislature's tax-rate-setting authority precisely because unilaterally setting their tax rates would contradict the equal-sovereignty principle stated here. That history confirms §20.2 functions as an operative limit other provisions must conform to, not just framing language.

The form-of-government bar is the provision's sharpest edged rule, and it guards against a particular failure mode: a Republic that, unable to dictate terms directly, instead uses the condition-of-association leverage to coerce internal restructuring of a nominally sovereign partner. Reading this under the Bad-Faith Test, the concern is that "equal sovereignty" could be hollowed out in practice if the Republic were still free to make association contingent on the Associated Community organizing its internal government a particular way — that would functionally recreate subordination through a back door even while nominally preserving sovereign-party status. By naming the prohibited act (requiring a particular form of government) and the prohibited mechanism (as a condition of association), the clause gives a concrete, checkable boundary rather than a vague aspiration.

This provision depends on §20.1's definition of what an Associated Community is — a sovereign political community that remains outside the Republic in a consensual compact relationship, available to recognized Indigenous nations and to independent nations outside the Republic. That definition is what makes "equal sovereign parties" a meaningful description rather than a label grafted onto a dependent entity. §20.2 also sits upstream of §20.7, which separately provides that compacts remain binding across a change of government and that amendment proceeds under the compact's own terms and applicable treaty procedures; §20.7 protects the compact's durability over time, while §20.2 fixes the character of the parties to it at formation, and the two operate as distinct safeguards rather than one implying the other's rule. Within the compact's permitted content, the provision is otherwise open-ended, allowing representation, consultation, and participation arrangements to be shaped by negotiation rather than fixed by this section.

§20.3.text:
§20.3 sets the substantive floor that every association compact must meet, and it does so by anchoring itself to a single external definition rather than restating rights language. Subsection (1) bars entry or ratification of any compact with an entity whose governance practices include, authorize, or systematically permit violations of the non-derogable rights listed in §1.16.a — torture, slavery, habeas corpus, public trial, the ban on retroactive punishment, and non-refoulement, plus the bar on discriminatory application of emergency measures. By pointing to §1.16.a instead of re-listing those rights, §20.3 keeps the substantive definition in one place and simply borrows it, which is the kind of structural economy that avoids duplicating a protection across multiple articles. The practical effect is a pre-ratification screen: an entity whose governance practices systematically permit these specific violations is simply ineligible for compact status, full stop, before any arbitration mechanism is ever invoked.

Once a compact exists, subsection (2) shifts enforcement to the compact's own independent arbitration mechanism — the same body §20.5 requires every compact to establish. Allegations of §1.16.a violations go to that mechanism, which may issue a preliminary determination triggering suspension, and the compact must itself provide procedures for urgent review and resolution of such disputes; the text does not supply a Republic-side emergency process, so the speed and shape of urgent review is built into each compact's own design rather than fixed uniformly here. Subsection (3) gives the same arbitration panel the power to terminate the compact where confirmed violations go unremedied within whatever period the compact specifies — again a compact-defined clock, not a constitutional deadline. This reliance on the compact's internal arbitration and its own procedural detail, rather than a centrally run tribunal, follows the Institution Test logic of routing enforcement through the body the parties already created under §20.5 instead of standing up a new constitutional enforcement apparatus for this one purpose.

Subsection (4) addresses a distinct and narrower concern: where an Associated Community's territory includes Indigenous nations with pre-existing governance relationships, the compact must address them, and it may not require their governance arrangements to be eliminated or diminished. This is a floor on compact content, not a condition on eligibility like subsection (1), and it guards against a compact being used to dissolve or override a pre-existing governance relationship as a side effect of integrating the Associated Community into the federation. Subsection (5) then clarifies that suspension's effects are governed by the compact's own terms, without prejudice to obligations independently binding under international law — so suspension under this provision doesn't erase separate international-law obligations the parties already carry. Read together with §20.4's bar on compelling continued association and §20.5's requirement that every compact build an arbitration mechanism in the first place, §20.3 functions as the substantive gatekeeping and remedial layer: it defines what disqualifies a compact from existing, what triggers suspension or termination once one exists, and what a compact may never bargain away regardless of the parties' consent.

§20.4.text:
Sovereign Mobility sits at the point where associated status could, in theory, harden into permanent subordination, and it closes that possibility by guaranteeing an exit. The provision gives the Associated Community itself — acting through whatever democratic or traditional governance process it uses — the sole authority to terminate its compact with the Republic. The Republic's role here is purely negative: it may neither prevent the decision nor penalize it. That structure reflects the Institution Test in a narrow sense — the community's own existing governance process is the vehicle for the decision, with no new body or approval mechanism inserted between the community's choice and its legal effect. Termination becomes effective according to the compact's own agreed procedures, triggered by written notice registered to the NRS. That NRS registration is the only administrative step named, and it functions as a transparency mechanism: the fact and timing of termination become part of the public record rather than a private or contested event, satisfying the Transparency Test by making the exercise of this authority visible without subjecting it to review or veto.

The provision's final sentence is its core structural safeguard: termination procedures, whatever the compact specifies, may not permit either party to compel the continued association of an unwilling sovereign community. This caps what the compact's own drafters can design into the relationship — no matter how the parties structure notice periods, phase-outs, or conditions in their termination procedures, those procedures cannot be used to trap either side in an association it no longer consents to. This is a floor, not a procedure in itself; it constrains what §20.4's "agreed procedures" clause can validly contain. Read against the Bad-Faith Test, this closes an obvious workaround: a party could otherwise write an exit process so burdensome or conditional that it never actually completes, achieving compelled association through procedural design rather than open refusal. By naming the result — no compelled continuation — rather than specifying the mechanics, the provision polices the compact's substance at a higher level than the procedural details it otherwise delegates to the compact.

This connects to the surrounding compact architecture in Article XX. §20.3 shows that termination is not the only way a compact can end — arbitration can terminate a compact for confirmed, unremedied rights violations — but that is an involuntary, violation-triggered mechanism controlled by the arbitration panel, distinct from the voluntary act Sovereign Mobility protects. §20.5's review and arbitration mechanisms govern disputes during an ongoing compact, while §20.4 governs its ending; the two are not redundant because one addresses mid-term grievances and the other addresses the relationship's termination. The guarded failure mode is straightforward: without this provision, an association compact could function as a one-way door, with the Republic (or the compact's own drafted terms) able to lock a community into a relationship that community has decided, through its own governance process, to leave. Sovereign Mobility ensures the compact remains what the Republic's associated-status framework presumes it to be — a relationship resting on continuing consent rather than permanent legal capture.

§20.5.text:
§20.5 embodies the principle that association between the Republic and an Associated Community rests on mutual, enforceable obligation rather than one-sided authority. By requiring that each compact "define the reciprocal obligations of the parties," the provision treats the relationship as a negotiated bargain between two parties of standing, not a delegation of power from the Republic downward. This connects directly to §20.2's framing of the compact relationship around equal sovereignty: reciprocity only makes sense as a structural commitment if the parties are understood as sovereign equals bargaining over mutual duties, not as a central government imposing terms on a subordinate unit.

The operative design choice is that neither party is left to interpret or enforce those obligations unilaterally. The provision requires each compact to "establish an independent arbitration mechanism," meaning the compact itself — not the Republic's ordinary courts or executive agencies — must specify a forum for resolving disputes. This mechanism is not optional or a fallback; it is a mandatory term of every compact, placed on the same footing as the reciprocal-obligations requirement itself. The practical effect is that disputes over compliance do not default to the Republic's own institutions, which could otherwise sit as both a party to the dispute and its judge. This is the same independent arbitration mechanism that §20.3 relies on for adjudicating alleged §1.16.a violations, preliminary suspension determinations, and confirmed-violation terminations — showing that the mechanism created under §20.5 is not a formality but the actual forum through which the Article's most serious compliance questions get decided.

The review clause supplies a distinct, lighter-weight mechanic: either party may request review of the compact by written notice registered to the NRS, with review procedures left entirely to the compact to establish. This is an ordinary, non-adversarial channel for revisiting compact terms, and it is procedurally separate from the arbitration mechanism and from the termination procedure in §20.4. Termination under §20.4 also runs through written notice registered to the NRS, but it rests on a different trigger (a unilateral decision through the Community's own governance process) and carries a different legal effect (ending the compact under its own agreed procedures). §20.5's review notice does not end anything by itself; it only triggers whatever review process the compact has set up, leaving the compact's substantive terms intact unless and until that process produces a change. Keeping review and termination as separate registered-notice mechanisms, each tied to its own trigger and consequence, prevents a party from invoking one process's effect under the other's label — for instance, treating a review request as grounds for exit, or treating an arbitration dispute as resolvable through ordinary review rather than the independent mechanism the compact is required to maintain. The guarded failure mode is thus a compact that defines obligations on paper but gives the stronger party — most plausibly the Republic — effective control over interpreting or enforcing them, defeating the equal-sovereignty premise the Article otherwise establishes.

§20.6.text:
§20.6 establishes that compacts with Associated Communities are negotiated and concluded by the Legat Consul but take legal effect only after Senate ratification under §3.6. This splits the compact power into two distinct functions: the Legat Consul's authority under §2.1, which covers foreign affairs and indigenous nation relations and vests operational decisions in that office, controls the negotiation and conclusion of the instrument; the Senate's ratification authority under §3.6 controls whether that instrument binds the Republic. Because an Associated Community is defined under §20.1 as a sovereign political community in a consensual compact relationship with the Republic, compacts under this Article function as the kind of international-style agreement that §3.6 treats as a treaty or compact agreement requiring ratification by two-thirds of the full seated Senate, rather than the lower threshold applicable to trade agreements. The text of §20.6 contains no independent ratification procedure of its own; it simply incorporates §3.6 by cross-reference, so the threshold, the chamber involved, and the amendment bar all come from §3.6 rather than from anything stated in Article XX.

This arrangement follows the same structural logic as the negotiate/ratify split applied to treaties generally: the Legat Consul, as the officer holding foreign-affairs authority, conducts the diplomatic work of reaching terms with the other sovereign party, while the Senate, as the body representing the States equally regardless of population, must affirmatively approve the result before it binds the Republic. Under §3.6, that ratification requires two-thirds of the full seated Senate, and once concluded, neither chamber may amend the terms of the agreement — ratification is an up-or-down check on the negotiated instrument, not an opportunity to rewrite it. The reliance on §3.6 rather than a freestanding Article XX procedure means compact ratification is not a separate invented mechanism; it reuses the same actor, the same chamber, and the same threshold already defined for treaties and compact agreements elsewhere in the constitution.

The design history for this provision records that an earlier version contained a JM (Judicial Monitor) prerequisite and a §9.1 reference, which were removed. The removal means the Legat Consul's authority to negotiate and conclude a compact is not conditioned on certification by the Judicial Monitor; the sole constitutional check on the compact is the Senate's ratification vote under §3.6. A separate audit action removed a JM assessment prerequisite and void rule from §20.3 and added an SC challenge mechanism there, specifically to resolve a direct conflict with §20.6 — confirming that §20.6's ratification pathway through the Senate, not a Judicial Monitor certification step, is the operative check on whether a negotiated compact becomes binding. Structurally, requiring Senate ratification guards against the Legat Consul unilaterally binding the Republic to a sovereign-to-sovereign arrangement without the Senate's consent, since compacts recognize Associated Communities as sovereign political communities outside the Republic and carry the same stakes as a treaty.

§20.7.text:
Compact Continuity embodies the principle that an association compact is an agreement between sovereigns, not a policy of whichever administration happens to hold office in the Republic at a given moment. Because §20.2 establishes the Republic and an Associated Community as equal sovereign parties to their compact, the compact's force cannot rest on the discretion of a particular government — it has to survive the ordinary churn of Republic politics, elections, and administrations. §20.7 supplies that guarantee directly: the compact remains binding on the Republic notwithstanding a change of government. This is a pre-political constraint rather than a policy choice, since it forecloses any future government from treating the compact as renegotiable simply because new officeholders prefer different terms.

The operative design choice is narrow and two-part. First, continuity is stated as an unconditional rule — no exception for new governments, no transitional carve-out, and no mechanism by which a change in Republic leadership alone unlocks amendment. Second, the provision does not freeze the compact forever; it routes change through two named channels — the compact's own terms and the applicable constitutional treaty procedures. This keeps the compact alive as binding law while still allowing it to evolve, but only through processes anchored outside the discretion of any single Republic administration. The practical effect is that a compact negotiated under one government cannot be reopened, reinterpreted, or quietly abandoned by a successor government acting unilaterally; any change has to run through whatever amendment or renegotiation mechanism the compact itself specifies, combined with the Republic's general treaty procedures.

§20.7 depends on §20.2 for its subject matter, since "the compact" it protects is the same equal-sovereign instrument that section defines, and it operates alongside §20.4's sovereign mobility rule without overlapping it: §20.4 governs how an Associated Community may unilaterally exit, while §20.7 governs how the Republic-side political cycle does not by itself disturb the compact's binding status or terms. The two provisions address different actors and different triggers — one a community's own governance process, the other a change of government — and neither transfers its trigger or procedure to the other. The failure mode §20.7 guards against is a Republic government using a change in administration as a backdoor to escape, dilute, or unilaterally rewrite compact obligations that were negotiated with an equal sovereign party. Without this provision, an incoming government could claim that commitments made by its predecessor do not bind it, treating the compact as ordinary policy subject to reversal rather than as a standing agreement between sovereigns — undermining the equal-sovereignty premise set out in §20.2 and leaving Associated Communities exposed to the instability of the Republic's own political cycle.
